description:
ExistingPatchesSection inlines every port/files/patch-* in the bundle with no
cap on how many. On www/chromium that is 1,604 patches and 93.5% of the
prompt, and it is the wrong 1,604: the overlay's own dragonfly/ patches are
not in the payload at all.

MEASURED — www_chromium-20260909-135208Z, patch attempt 1 session

  payload (one user message)   2,056,421 chars   ~514,105 tok
  "### Existing Patches"       1,921,730 chars   ~480,432 tok   93.5%
    1,604 #### subsections, runs to end of payload
  everything else                134,691 chars    ~33,672 tok    6.5%

Bundle artifact count for port/files/patch-* is 1,604 — one per subsection.

COST

Three chromium patch attempts, from runner.log llm_turn accounting:

  attempt   turns   billable     output   full cache misses   miss cost
  1            92   2,242,243        3%    3                  1,959,653  87%
  2            58   5,365,245        1%    8                  5,255,552  98%
  3           154   5,532,226        2%    6                  4,645,529  84%
                   ----------                                 ---------
                   13,139,714                                 ~11.9M

Model output is 1-3% of spend. Everything else is re-sent input, and a
re-send costs 620-840k because the payload is that big. 17 misses did it.

Cache behaviour itself does not look controllable from here: misses follow
gaps as short as 33s and hits as long as 173s, after every kind of tool, so
it is not a TTL and not tied to the ~5 min dsynth_build. Payload size is the
part we own.

THE PER-FILE CAP DOES NOT HELP

runner.context_file_cap = 32768. Across the 1,604 subsections: median 780
chars, mean 1,198, max 26,376. Zero were truncated. The cap was added for
the opposite shape -- PortFilesSection's docstring cites python311's 533 KB
pkg-plist -- and a per-file cap cannot see 1,604 individually-reasonable
files. There is no section-level or payload-level budget.

THE SELECTION IS ALSO WRONG

context.py:472 filters on p.startswith("port/files/patch-"). For chromium:

  composed files/       1606 (1604 patch-*, plus chrome.in, chromium-browser.desktop.in)
  composed dragonfly/    144
  in both                 96   ours overriding a FreeBSD patch of the same name
  dragonfly-only          48
  bundle port/dragonfly/   0

So the agent is shipped 1,604 FreeBSD patches and none of the overlay's own.
Spot-checked four dragonfly-only patches (patch-base_process_launch__posix.cc
and three others): none appear in the payload. For the 96 shared names it
sees the FreeBSD content, not the DragonFly override that the port actually
carries. A patch agent working on a DragonFly overlay is being shown
everything except the DragonFly patches.

WHAT THE AGENT ACTUALLY USED

Same session, its own retrieval across 92 turns:

  get_file               14 calls    ~14,772 tok
  grep                   15 calls    ~19,504 tok
  get_effective_overlay   1 call      ~4,109 tok
  dops_reference          1 call      ~3,088 tok
  list_dir                2 calls       ~402 tok
  TOTAL                  33 calls    ~41,876 tok

It has the tools and uses them. Fetching on demand costs ~42k against
~480k for inlining everything up front.

FIX DIRECTION

- Give the section a total budget, not just a per-file one, and prefer a
  manifest over bodies past that budget: 1,604 filenames is ~50k chars
  (~12k tok) against ~480k for the contents.
- Include the overlay's dragonfly/ patches, and where a name exists in both,
  show the one that governs.
- Consider ordering by relevance to the failing build rather than sorted()
  when a budget forces a choice.

Payload would drop ~514k -> ~35k, making every cache miss ~15x cheaper. The
same three attempts fit inside the old 5M tier budget with room to spare.
Note this also bounds the value of raising policy.tiers.ASSIST.max_tokens to
30M (done 2026-09-09): at 800k a miss that mostly buys more expensive misses.

CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER READING

Splitting www/chromium's monolithic dragonfly/patch-all into 142 per-file
patches (2026-09-09) did NOT contribute. Those live in dragonfly/, which the
payload does not include. The 1,604 are FreeBSD's own and predate it.
design:
REVISED after looking at what other harnesses do. The first draft proposed
"budget + rank + inline until the budget is spent". That is still the wrong
shape. No comparable harness pushes file bodies into the prompt at all.

WHY runner.context_file_cap IS THE WRONG PRIMITIVE

It is used in exactly one place -- context.py -- i.e. only on content pushed
into the prompt unasked. The pull side already does the right thing:
get_file takes limit_lines plus start_line/end_line, which is ordinary
pagination.

A per-file cap on pushed content fails twice over:
  - it cannot bound the total. 1,604 files x median 780 chars = 480k tokens,
    every one of them under the 32,768 cap, zero truncated.
  - when it does fire it hands the model a head+tail splice of a file it
    never asked for, with no way to know what was elided.

PRIOR ART

Aider (aider.chat/2023/10/22/repomap.html) does not inline files. It builds a
repo MAP: a graph of symbol definitions and references, personalized PageRank
to rank by relevance, then renders top-ranked DEFINITIONS -- signatures, not
bodies -- binary-searched to fit a token budget that defaults to 1k tokens.
We spend 480k on the same job.

SWE-agent (arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793) rejects inlining explicitly: "Flooding a
language agent's context window with too much file content can be
inefficient, since the majority of file content is usually irrelevant to the
issue," and notes such inefficiency "can exhaust an agent's cost budget or
context window, leading to even worse performance." It gives the agent
windowed viewing (100-line windows) with scroll/goto instead.

Claude Code, Pi and OpenClaw cap file READS -- 256KB stat check, 2,000 lines
or 50KB -- and pair the cap with offset/limit pagination, persisting
oversized results outside the context. The cap belongs on what a tool
returns when asked, which is where ours already is for get_file.

On truncation as such: "Truncation that's too aggressive isn't just lossy --
it's misleadingly lossy, because the agent has no way to know it's missing
the relevant span."

REVISED FIX

1. ExistingPatchesSection emits a MANIFEST, not bodies. Names only, grouped,
   with the dragonfly/ override marked where a basename exists in both. For
   chromium that is ~1,604 names (~50k chars) or, better, per-directory
   counts plus the paths -- against 1,921,730 chars today.

2. No inlined bodies by default. The measured case for inlining is empty:
   in attempt 1 the agent made 14 get_file calls and read NONE of the 1,604
   patches. It read overlay.dops, the port Makefile, Mk/Features/lto.mk,
   bootstrap.py, gen.py, libcxx22/newport/Makefile -- several with
   start_line/end_line. It fetches precisely when it wants something.

3. Name the location. The manifest should give the composed port path
   (/work/artifacts/compose/@2026Q3/<origin>/files and .../dragonfly) so
   get_file and list_dir reach the real files. The agent already reads live
   chroot paths, so it needs no bundle artifact to see a patch.

4. Leave runner.context_file_cap alone for PULLED results, and stop using it
   as if it were a section budget. If a pushed section ever needs a bound,
   it needs a section-level budget, not a per-file one -- but per 2, the
   right bound here is zero bodies.

5. Optional, later: if orientation beyond names proves useful, the Aider
   shape is the model -- rank by relevance to the failing build (patches
   whose target path appears in logs/errors.txt), and render something
   smaller than a body, e.g. the ---/+++ header and hunk count.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE

Layer 1 stands: hook_pkg_failure has no dragonfly/ loop, so no bundle has
port/dragonfly/ artifacts and the overlay's own patches are invisible. That
is a correctness bug independent of the token question, and a manifest that
lists only port/files/ would still be wrong.

EXPECTED EFFECT

Payload 514k -> ~35k plus a names list. Cache misses ~15x cheaper. The three
attempts that cost 13.1M fit inside the old 5M tier budget. And per
SWE-agent's finding, less irrelevant content should improve the agent's
behaviour, not merely its cost.

description:
The proof-block orphan rescue in attempt_loop cannot tell "no proof block
emitted" from "proof block emitted saying false", so it overrides an explicit
gave-up report and resolves the bundle agent_fixed.

OBSERVED

www_chromium-20260909-135208Z, patch attempt 1. The agent's own analysis/patch.md:

  ## Rebuild Status
  gave-up

  ## Rebuild Proof (JSON)
  { "rebuild_ok": false }

and in its summary: "the link then fails on undefined reference to
'__cxa_thread_atexit' ... which I could not resolve within this attempt".

The agent was correct and honest. What got written was
analysis/rebuild_proof.json:

  { "rebuild_ok": true, "source": "tool_result", ... }

and the bundle resolved resolution=agent_fixed on a port whose last
dsynth_build returned rebuild_ok=False.

MECHANISM

attempt_loop.py:592-612

    proof = _parse(prev_text)
    rebuild_ok = bool(_ok(proof))
    ...
    if not rebuild_ok and rebuild_ok_seen and is_success is None:
        proof = {"rebuild_ok": True, "source": "tool_result"}
        rebuild_ok = True

Two problems.

1. `not rebuild_ok` is satisfied by BOTH an absent proof block and a proof
   block that explicitly says false. The comment above the branch only
   contemplates the first ("the LLM may have run out of budget before it
   could emit ## Rebuild Proof (JSON)"). Nothing distinguishes them, so an
   explicit negative is silently upgraded.

2. `is_success is None` reads like a status guard but is not one. It is the
   optional custom success-predicate parameter, None for every patch run
   (convert passes its own). It never blocks anything here.

`rebuild_ok_seen` is also sticky for the whole attempt. Here it was set at
14:22:40 by a dsynth_build that returned rebuild_ok=True after 4 seconds --
against ~5 minutes for the real builds in the same attempt -- then survived
four subsequent FAIL builds over the next 30 minutes to arm the rescue at
14:54:43. Even a rescue that only fired on a genuinely absent proof would be
lifting a stale True.

RELATION TO poly-qkp

Same rescue, same synthesized {"rebuild_ok": true, "source": "tool_result"},
same bogus agent_fixed. poly-qkp is the attempt hitting the turn cap so no
final report exists -- the case the branch was written for. This is the
branch firing against a report that exists and says gave-up. A fix that only
addresses the turn-cap path leaves this one open, and vice versa; most
likely both want the same repair.

FIX DIRECTION

- Distinguish absent proof from negative proof. Only rescue when _parse
  returned nothing at all; never when it returned rebuild_ok=false.
- Do not lift a stale rebuild_ok_seen. If the rescue is kept, gate it on the
  MOST RECENT dsynth_build result, not on any-time-during-the-attempt.
- Rename or remove the `is_success is None` clause; it does not do what it
  reads as.

SECONDARY, NOT VERIFIED

Why the 14:22:40 build exited 0 in 4 seconds is unconfirmed. rebuild_ok is
p.returncode == 0 (worker.py:3264, identical in the installed copy on the
builder) with no guard for dsynth ignoring or skipping a port rather than
compiling it, and tools.py:169 asserts to the model that "rebuild_ok=true
means rc==0, i.e. it built AND passed the gate". The ignore/skip hypothesis
has NOT been tested; the per-port log was overwritten by later attempts and
agent builds run hooks-disabled, so nothing was recorded. Confirm before
acting.
title: the proof-block orphan rescue overrides an explicit rebuild_ok:false, so a gave-up attempt still reports agent_fixed

description:
A `type dport` port can never be classified `converted`, so the patch flow
escalates every successful fix on one. Affects 88 ports.

WHAT HAPPENED (devel/libcxx22, 2026-09-08)

  bundle devel_libcxx22-20260908-224530Z
  patch job 20260908-225449Z-2026Q3-devel_libcxx22-554173-patch.job

check-plist failed (577 `Error: Orphaned:` + 1 `Error: Missing:`). The agent
edited `ports/devel/libcxx22/newport/pkg-plist` -- the correct and only
surface for a dport -- adding exactly the 577 orphans and removing the 1
missing entry. Rebuild passed: rebuild_ok=True, patch status=success.

It was then escalated:

  Reason: patch_non_dops_substrate
  Detail: build passed but port dops_state='needs_judgment'
          (expected 'converted'); fix likely written as compat artifacts
          instead of overlay.dops

That detail is false. There are no compat artifacts; the agent edited the
only file that exists. Cost: 963,612 billable over 213 turns, discarded.

MECHANISM

The gate is steps.py:1415:

    post_state = ctx.state.get("post_patch_dops_state")
    if post_state != "converted":
        ... ESCALATE_MANUAL, reason="patch_non_dops_substrate"

Correct for a `type port`: a build that went green by editing a leftover
Makefile.DragonFly is not a dops fix and should not be stamped agent_fixed.

`post_patch_dops_state` comes from classify_dops -> assess_overlay
(overlay_state.py). There, `newport/` is counted as an unmigrated legacy
artifact:

    overlay_state.py:245   unmigrated = (... + (("newport/",) if facts.newport else ()))
    overlay_state.py:294   "legacy_newport_present", severity="conversion_blocker"
    overlay_state.py:298   invariants.append("dops_with_unmigrated_newport")
    overlay_state.py:299   if not unmigrated: return state="converted"

For a `type port`, a stray `newport/` genuinely is an unfinished migration.
For a `type dport`, `newport/` IS the port, permanently and by design -- the
overlay.dops is a 4-line header with zero ops. So a fully and correctly
migrated dport is indistinguishable from a half-migrated normal port, and
line 299 is unreachable for any of them.

ROOT CAUSE: MISSING INPUT, NOT A WRONG COMPARISON

OverlayFacts (overlay_state.py:35) records only presence:

    overlay_dops: bool = False     # not the declared type
    newport: bool = False

The declared `type` never reaches the assessor, so it cannot distinguish the
two cases even in principle. The planner already extracts it
(engine/planner.py:444-452, TypeDirective -> plan_type).

The same file knows the right answer 200 lines earlier. The bootstrap
decision at overlay_state.py:89-94:

    # A pure dport: newport/ is the whole port -- declare type=dport, drop
    # the now-redundant STATUS (the header carries the type).
    if facts.newport:
        return BootstrapDecision("bootstrap", overlay_type="dport", ...)

So the code can author a dport correctly and then cannot recognise the thing
it authored.

BLAST RADIUS

88 ports in DeltaPorts declare `type dport`, and all 88 have `newport/`
(grep -l '^type dport' ports/*/*/overlay.dops). None can reach `converted`,
so the agent can never auto-fix any of them however correct the fix -- it
will always build green and then escalate with a misleading accusation.

SUGGESTED FIX

1. Carry the declared overlay type into OverlayFacts (parse the `type`
   directive; planner.py already does this).
2. In assess_overlay, exclude `newport/` from `unmigrated` and from the
   `conversion_blocker` rule when the declared type is `dport`.
3. Keep both when the declared type is `port` -- that case is a real
   unfinished migration and the existing guard is right.
4. Consider flagging the inverse (`type dport` with NO newport/) since that
   overlay declares a source tree that does not exist.

The steps.py:1415 gate itself needs no change once the classification is
right.

NOTE ON THE ESCALATION TEXT

Even after the classification is fixed, `patch_non_dops_substrate`'s detail
string asserts a cause ("fix likely written as compat artifacts") it has not
checked. Worth making it name the artifacts it actually found, so a wrong
diagnosis is visible rather than plausible.
title: assess_overlay counts newport/ as unmigrated, so no type-dport port can reach 'converted' and every successful dport patch escalates

description:
In dops-mode compose the compat auto-copy is suppressed
(compose_stages.py:832, `if ctx.mode != "compat": continue`, surfaced as
I_COMPOSE_MODE_DOPS_SUPPRESSES_COMPAT). A file under dragonfly/ therefore
reaches the build ONLY via an explicit `file materialize` op.

Nothing tells the agent when that op is missing. The patch phase cannot
fail on it -- a patch that is not in the composed tree is not applied, and
not applying is not an error -- so the build proceeds and fails for the
original reason. From the agent's side the fix "did not work".

THREE INSTANCES THIS WEEK

1. multimedia/v4l_compat (2026-09-06). Agent wrote the patch, omitted the
   materialize op, and the bundle read as an incomplete fix.

2. www/firefox run 2 (2026-09-07). patch-tools_profiler_lul_LulElfInt.h
   created, not materialized. Caught in review before commit; the composed
   tree had 7 patches where dragonfly/ had 8.

3. www/firefox run 4 (2026-09-08). THE EXPENSIVE ONE.
   patch-config_gcc-stl-wrapper.template.h created, not materialized. The
   agent then spent its last three rounds -- roughly two hours of wall
   clock -- trying variants that landed in the *generated* wrapper headers
   instead, because its correct approach (patch the template that
   generates them) appeared not to work. It never reached a build.

WHAT EXISTS TODAY, AND WHY IT DOES NOT COVER THIS

dportsv3/agent/reconcile.py handles the OPPOSITE direction: when an edit
removes a materialize op and strands its file, reconcile_orphaned_artifacts
deletes the file. Its docstring is explicit that an unreferenced artifact
is "inert ... it does no harm to the build, but it lingers as dead
substrate".

That is true for a stranded file. It is not true for a NEW file: there the
inertness is the whole problem, because the agent believes it applied a fix.

It also runs too late to help. steps.py:1323:

    if (result.status or "").lower() == "success":
        ...
        removed = reconcile_orphaned_artifacts(port_dir)

Success-only, after the attempt, before the diff is captured. A failing
attempt never reaches it, which is exactly the case where the missing op

design:
Wanted: a signal DURING the attempt, at the moment the agent would
otherwise start a 45-minute build against a tree that does not contain its
change.

Natural home is validate_dops or materialize_dports -- the agent already
calls both, and materialize_dports is the last step before dsynth_build in
practically every round. Either could report:

    dragonfly/ contains 35 files; overlay.dops has 34 `file materialize`
    ops. Unreferenced: patch-config_gcc-stl-wrapper.template.h
    (this file will NOT be applied).

Two design points:

- Warn, do not block. An unreferenced file is legitimate when the agent is
  deliberately retiring a patch -- www/firefox run 5 did exactly that,
  removing the materialize op for a patch it had proved could not work.
  Blocking would have prevented the correct action.

- Distinguish the two directions if cheap. "New file, no op" is nearly
  always a mistake; "op removed, file stranded" is the case reconcile.py
  already cleans up. The wording should not tell the agent to re-add an op
  it deliberately deleted.

The invariant is simply: count(dragonfly/*) == count(`^file materialize`),
and naming the difference is enough. Every instance above would have been
caught by that one line.

tool_loop.run appends and never removes. The only mutations of the message
list are:

  tool_loop.py:233   messages.append(_assistant_message_from(response))
  tool_loop.py:293   messages.append(...)

No prune, no cap, no elision anywhere in the file. Context therefore grows
monotonically for the life of an attempt, and since every dsynth_build
outlives the prompt cache, the cost of each build round is whatever the
context has reached by then.

MEASURED (www/firefox, 2026-09-07/08)

  run 4, attempt 1     78k at T1  ->  185k at T106  ->  348k at T124
                       per-eviction cost rose with it, ~140k -> ~348k

  run 3, attempt 1     166k, then one oversized dsynth_log took it to
                       857k, and every later eviction cost ~860k
                       (see poly-9hjm for that call)

Attempts currently get their context reset only by ending. That works --
run 3 attempt 2 restarted at 80,697 after attempt 1 reached 314,527 -- but
it is a reset, not a compaction: everything is re-derived from the bundle,
which is why the first turns of an attempt re-read files the previous
attempt had already read.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW

runner.max_tool_turns is 300 in the live config. A 300-turn attempt on a
big port does ~15 build rounds; with unbounded growth the last rounds cost
several times the first. The turn cap is only usable if the per-turn cost
does not climb with turn number.
design:
THE POLICY IS ALREADY WRITTEN

fix_chat.render_session_transcript (fix_chat.py:101) does exactly the
right thing, and its docstring states the reasoning:

    "When over cap, keeps the head and tail and elides the middle: the
     head holds the failure + triage + first-move reasoning, the tail
     holds the winning approach + rebuild proof -- both are what 'why'
     questions hinge on. The repeated middle build cycles are the most
     expendable. Whole-block, so no turn is cut mid-sentence (a single
     oversized block is head+tail clipped first)."

DEFAULT_CONTEXT_CAP = 96 * 1024 (fix_chat.py:31).

It is only reached from the tracker's fix-review chat --
agentic_api.py:373 via build_chat_messages -- which is a tools-off Q&A
over frozen artifacts. The loop that actually accumulates context never
uses it.

"The repeated middle build cycles are the most expendable" describes a
300-turn porting attempt more accurately than it describes the review
chat.

WHY THIS IS CHEAP

fix_chat's elision is pure text/block manipulation. It costs nothing to
run. Claude-Code-style compaction by summarisation would cost one full
context read to apply -- at 860k that is a 17% tax just to shrink.

CARE NEEDED

- fix_chat renders tool_calls as text because it runs tools-off. A live
  loop must keep the structured tool_call/tool_result pairing intact, so
  elision has to drop whole call+result pairs, not rewrite them.
- Dropping a tool result the model still refers to will confuse it. The
  head/tail shape helps (recent turns survive) but the boundary needs
  thought.
- Interacts with worker's "you already have this" dedup
  (reset_attempt_caches, worker.py:1352): if an elided file read is later
  deduped as already-seen, the model is refused content it no longer has.
  That failure mode is already documented in attempt_loop.py:399.
notes:
REVISED 2026-09-16: mask old tool output, don't drop exchanges.

1294712 (unpushed) did the first design: over a byte cap, leave the oldest
whole exchanges out of the request. The literature says that is the variant
nobody uses: it deletes the agent's actions and its failed turns.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS

- JetBrains, "The Complexity Trap" (arXiv 2508.21433, NeurIPS'25 DL4Code).
  SWE-agent and OpenHands on SWE-bench Verified, five model setups.
  Replacing tool observations older than the last 10 turns with a
  placeholder, while keeping every reasoning step and action, cut cost
  by more than half and matched or beat LLM summarization in 4 of 5
  settings (Qwen3-Coder: +2.6 points solved, 52% cheaper). Summarization
  made agents run 15% longer, cost up to 7% on its own, and got almost no
  cache reuse. The window is agent-specific and must be tuned.
- Anthropic clear_tool_uses_20250919: keep the calls, replace old results
  with a placeholder, keep=3 by default, exclude_tools, and clear_at_least
  so each cache invalidation is worth paying for. Clearing +29%, clearing
  plus the memory tool +39% on their agentic-search eval.
- Manus: prompt-cache hit rate is the top cost metric; append-only
  context; restorable compression (drop content, keep the path); keep
  failed turns visible.
- Server-side context editing and compaction are out of reach: the
  harness calls chat.completions / litellm on OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

GAP SPECIFIC TO THIS HARNESS

Masking relies on the model's reasoning surviving it. In misc/py-onnx
(2026-09-16) 0 of 138 assistant turns stored reasoning_content and 19 had
any text, so masked outputs would take the why with them. The literature's
answer is note-taking (Anthropic's memory tool, Manus's todo.md).

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED

Masking when a slow tool call has probably let the cache expire, to make
the mask free. Measured on py-onnx: 60-120s calls preceded a miss 2 times
in 10, and 5 misses followed no long call at all. Not predictable enough.

DESIGN

1. tool_loop masks tool results older than llm.patch.context_keep_turns
   (default 10) with a fixed placeholder that keeps ok/rebuild_ok and says
   to repeat the call. Calls are never masked. messages, and so the
   session dump, keep everything; only the request is masked.
2. Batched: mask once llm.patch.context_mask_batch bytes (32KB) of old
   output are maskable, so the cached prefix holds between masks.
3. dops_reference and note are never masked. A mask resets get_file's
   scroll-back dedup.
4. note(text): the agent records why a build failed. Calls are never
   masked, and the retry hand-over carries the notes to the next attempt.
5. No LLM summarization until a measured need.

MEASURE: observations_masked (count, bytes, turn), repeat_after_mask (a
read repeated after its output was masked), turns per attempt, cost,
rebuild_ok rate.
REVIEWED 2026-09-16 (still uncommitted, on top of 1294712)

• Placeholders said "Repeat the call" for every tool. Repeating dsynth_build rebuilds; repeating edit_file applies the edit twice. Only reads say it now; dsynth_build points at dsynth_log, edit_file/put_file at get_file.
• Results under 512 bytes are not masked. On py-onnx they were 46 of 160 results and 4% of the bytes: validate_dops diagnostics, refused writes, edit confirmations. Masking them saved 2%.
• An empty note is refused. The hand-over carries at most 20 notes, 500 chars each. runner.log shows the note text.

  mask 10 turns/32KB/512B   peak  82k  sent  8.5M  on 9 real misses 597k  + 107k re-billed by 7 masks
  (without the 512B floor:  peak  81k  sent  8.3M)

NOT DONE: notes stop at the job. A later job's Prior Attempts section (context.py) shows the last 12 trace events and renders a note with no text.

description:
worker.dsynth_log (worker.py:3310) is

    def dsynth_log(env, origin, tail_lines: int = 200, flavor: str = "")

and truncates purely by line count:

    if tail_lines > 0 and len(lines) > tail_lines:

        kept = lines[-tail_lines:]

size is unbounded for a log whose lines are long.

WHAT HAPPENED (www/firefox, 2026-09-07, bundle
www_firefox-20260907-104857Z)

The agent called dsynth_log and got 4301 lines back. firefox's failing
build log is mostly cargo verbose output, whose `Running `CARGO=...`` lines
are multiple KB each. Measured from runner.log:

  12:15:49  [tool:dsynth_log] origin=www/firefox lines=4301 ok
  A1.T82    in=849,927 (cached=166,385)  billable=684,329

to ~857k and stayed there, so every subsequent cache eviction cost ~860k
instead of ~140k. Every dsynth_build evicts (the call outlives the TTL),

  A1.T98   billable=859,775
  A1.T105  billable=863,000 (approx)

attempt was 41,116 tokens -- 1.55% of spend.

grep (worker.py:1213) caps at max_bytes=8192 and says why:

    "The token cost difference between 'matches + a few context lines'
     and 'the whole 200KB Makefile.in' is the difference between
     affordable and not."

dsynth_log has the same exposure and no such cap.

COUNTERFACTUAL

The next run (2026-09-08) asked for 39-99 line tails. Context stayed at
~140k, evictions cost ~140k, and the same 5M covered roughly 7x more build
rounds.
design:
The helper already exists. worker.py:125:

    def _tail(s: str, max_bytes: int = _MAX_STREAM_BYTES) -> tuple[str, bool]

with _MAX_STREAM_BYTES = 32_768 (worker.py:122). It is used for diff
output at worker.py:1197 but not by dsynth_log.

Smallest fix: pass dsynth_log's assembled tail through _tail() before
returning, and report byte truncation alongside the existing line
truncation so the agent knows it was cut.

Worth considering as well:

- Clamp tail_lines to a sane ceiling rather than trusting the caller.
- The tool's own docstring could state the cost, since the model chooses
  the argument. A one-line "keep this at the default unless you have a
  reason" is cheap and would have prevented this instance.

Sizing: a 32KB cap is ~8k tokens, comparable to grep's 8192-byte cap at
2k. Either is far below the 690k this cost.
notes:
CONSTRAINT ON THE FIX: the cap must be a raisable DEFAULT, not a hard ceiling.

Measured the opposite failure on devel/libcxx22 (2026-09-08, bundle
devel_libcxx22-20260908-224530Z, patch job ...-554173-patch.job).

check-plist failed with 578 enumerated error lines -- 577 `Error: Orphaned:`
plus 1 `Error: Missing:`. For a plist-error the log IS the fix: it names
every discrepancy exactly. The agent called dsynth_log at turn 10 and got
199 lines back (the 200 default), tail-anchored, so it saw the end of the
orphan list and none of the __cxx03/__algorithm/* bulk at the start.

It then spent ~40 turns and ~250k billable reconstructing that list from the
extracted source tree (grep 'cxx03|assertion_handler|\.imp|cxxabi|tr1|
__config_site|clang-format', reading libcxx/utils/libcxx/header_info and the
libcxxabi dir) -- deriving what the log had already printed in full. Reading
all 578 lines would have cost roughly 25k.

`truncated: true` and `total_lines`, so the agent was told it had a partial
view and could have re-asked. That half is agent guidance (the
error-plist-mismatch playbook never says to read the whole check-plist
block), filed separately.

What it does constrain here: if the byte cap this bead asks for is a hard
ceiling, the firefox fix makes the libcxx22 case permanently unreadable --
a large structured error block is exactly the content worth spending tokens
on, and it is not distinguishable by size from 4301 lines of cargo noise.
The two cases differ by INTENT, not volume. So:

  - byte cap = default, overridable by an explicit caller argument
  - keep returning truncated/total_lines so the caller can size a re-read
  - consider making the truncation head+tail or marker-anchored rather than
    tail-only, so a truncated read of an error block still shows its start

description:
worker.dsynth_build (worker.py:3270) runs `dsynth -S -y test`, which
force-rebuilds by design. On a large port that is the whole compile every
time, however small the edit.

MEASURED on www/firefox this week (2026-09-06..08), 5 runs:

  build round wall clock    ~45 min   (39:33 - 45:38 across ~20 rounds)
  token cost per round      ~380k     (the tool call outlives the prompt
                                       cache, so the turn that reads the
                                       result re-sends the whole context)

Run 5's winning attempt spent 2 rounds on a hypothesis that a 30-second
incremental compile would have refuted. Run 4 spent 3 consecutive rounds
(2h15m) re-testing one inert value.

The wall-clock cost and the token cost have the same root: the tool call
takes minutes, so every round evicts the prompt cache. A build that
finished in seconds would stay inside the TTL and cost ~2k instead of
~380k.

dsynth already supports the substrate:

  test   [ports] - 'build' w/DEVELOPER=yes and pre-deletes pkgs
  debug  [ports] - like 'test' but leaves mounts intact

`debug` leaves /construction/<origin> and the builder mounts in place, so
an incremental `gmake` in the existing objdir is possible without dsynth
re-entering. This was used by hand during the node24 SIGSEGV work to keep
a core file and its tree alive.
design:
SHAPE

  1. dsynth debug once per attempt, leaving the worker mounted.
  2. A new tool -- build_incremental(origin) -- runs gmake in the existing
     /construction/<origin>/.build and returns the compiler output.
  3. dsynth_build (test) stays exactly as it is, and remains the ONLY
     source of rebuild_ok.

_dsynth_run (worker.py:3182) is already parameterised by subcommand, so
the dsynth side is small.

WHY THIS IS NOT A poly-9sw REGRESSION

poly-9sw removed a second tool because dsynth_test and dsynth_build both
did a full build -- test measured at 103% of build on a port that
compiles, i.e. the same work twice for ~3% more signal. An incremental
gmake is not a second full build; it is a partial compile of what changed.

WHY THIS MUST NOT BECOME A poly-8ni REGRESSION

poly-8ni: the loop's success oracle (dsynth build) diverged from the
acceptance gate (dsynth test with DEVELOPER=1), so DEVELOPER/QA defects
passed the loop and failed verify. An incremental build is an even weaker
oracle than dsynth build was.

The constraint that keeps this safe: build_incremental must be a
DIAGNOSTIC, never an oracle. It answers "does this TU compile now"; it
must not set rebuild_ok, must not resolve a bundle, and the attempt must
still end on a dsynth_build (test) that passes. Stale objects can and will
lie -- that is acceptable for iteration and unacceptable for a verdict.

OPEN QUESTIONS

- Exclusivity: a held debug worker blocks the builder. Needs a lock and a
  release path, and interacts with the feeder.
- The stale-compose guard in _dsynth_run (baseline from
  _MATERIALIZE_STATE) needs an equivalent, or incremental builds will run
  against un-composed edits.
- Cleanup if an attempt dies with the worker still mounted.
title: Every agent build round costs a full dsynth test (~45 min, ~380k tokens); dsynth debug could make iteration incremental

It reaches both policy levels (bundle_actions/issue_actions and action_allowed/issue_action_allowed) and every mutating handler refuses anonymously at entry with 403 rather than a state or validation error. description:
Clarified 2026-09-05: "read-only" means ANONYMOUS — unauthenticated
people who want to see how the build is going. Not a user account with a
viewer role. Roughly 10 operators, several dozen anonymous readers.

This is a DESIGN constraint on every view, to be honoured now, not a
feature that waits for authentication to exist. Auth is the mechanism
(poly-fij.5) and can land later; the page composition it will switch
between has to be designed up front, because retrofitting it means
writing every template twice.

ONE CAPABILITY, NOT A ROLE SYSTEM

Templates take a single boolean — can_operate — resolved once per
request. No user table, no role model, no permissions matrix is needed
to design or build this. Today it is forced True for everyone, so
behaviour is unchanged. The day poly-fij.5 lands it is derived from the
session and nothing else moves.

FAIL CLOSED

The default is anonymous. Authentication GRANTS capability; it never
restricts it. A missing or unrecognised session must render the public
page, not the operator one. Written this way, the tracker becoming
publicly reachable before auth lands is a configuration decision rather
than an accident.

THREE TIERS, NOT TWO

Naming them now because page composition depends on it:

1. Public status — anonymous. Active builds, history, per-run results,
   port detail, compare, target diff, the run view, pipeline inventory
   counts, and which issues exist and what state they are in. This is
   the "how is the build going" surface and it is the default landing.
2. Operator actions — every mutating control: accept, reject, discard,
   retry, take-over, release, reopen, deliver, mute, resolve,
   cancel-build, verify, env selection, manual context submission.
3. Agent internals — the session viewer, fix-chat, tool trace and token
   accounting. Not mutating, but agent working material rather than
   build status. Decide per surface whether anonymous sees it; the
   default should be no.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE TEMPLATES

The action surface must be a SEPARABLE REGION in every view — one
omittable block — not controls interleaved through status panels. If it
is interleaved it cannot be omitted later without a rewrite. This is the
whole reason the bead lands before UI-1.

Concrete consequences already visible in the mock:

- UI-6's four tabs are audience-dependent. Fix and Evidence are public;
  Chat and History (sessions, tool trace, token cost) are tier 3. An
  anonymous cockpit has two tabs, not four.
- UI-5's queue shows bands and state to anyone; the per-row action and
  take-over are tier 2.
- The shell's secondary nav differs: Manual and Runner are operator
  destinations.
- UI-2 has no mutating actions at all, so Builds is identical for both
  audiences. That is a reason / serves Builds, not just a kit
  preference.

BOTH LEVELS, STILL

The policy is two-level by design: ACTION_ALLOWED is the authoritative
endpoint gate, bundle_actions() / issue_actions() are the deliberately
narrower UI surface. can_operate has to reach both. A hidden button in
front of a live POST endpoint is a hidden button, not read-only.

Nothing in fix_state.py or issue_state.py has any notion of an actor
today; ACTION_ALLOWED keys purely on resolution and verification_status.
There is no Depends, Authorization or session anywhere in the tracker.

description:
Two per-render costs the redesign multiplies. Both are cheap to fix and
neither needs an architecture change (see the process-model bead under
poly-fij for that).

ARTIFACT RENDERS ARE UNCACHED

render/artifacts.py decompresses up to MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES (4 MiB)
and UTF-8 decodes it on every request. No cache anywhere. The cockpit
gives evidence its own tab and switches between artifacts in place, so
the same log gets decompressed repeatedly in one sitting.

Blobs are content-addressed: artifact_refs carries sha256 and put_blob
already computes it. That is a free, perfect cache key — the bytes for
a sha can never change. A bounded LRU keyed on (sha256, render mode)
removes the repeat work with no invalidation problem.

THE QUEUE RENDER DOES DELIVERY RECONCILIATION

/agentic loops open_delivery_bundle_ids() and calls
delivery_sync.reconcile_bundle_delivery() per bundle, inside the
request, before reading issues. Each call opens its own connection
("self-contained connection management so both page routes can call
it").

It is throttled at DEFAULT_MIN_INTERVAL_S = 300, so it does not hammer
GitHub. The cost is per-render connection setup and latency on the one
endpoint UI-5 wants to poll live. A queue that refreshes every few
seconds should not carry a reconciliation loop.

Move it: a background sweep, or a separate endpoint the page calls at a
slower cadence than the queue itself.

ALREADY RIGHT, KEEP IT

agentic_bundle_artifact_fragment renders only the detail pane from the
same _artifact_detail.html partial the full page uses — one renderer,
no drift, no full-page re-render on artifact switch. The redesign
should extend that pattern, not replace it.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-06.

ARTIFACT CACHE. Byte-bounded LRU in render/artifacts.py keyed on
(sha256, relpath, kind), guarded by a lock because the tracker serves on
a threadpool. Measured on a 3 MB gzipped log: 57 ms cold, 0.0 ms warm.

Three details the bead did not settle:
• The key is (sha256, relpath, kind), not (sha256, render mode). The same
  bytes render differently under a different name -- a diff is not a log
  -- so the name is part of the identity, and 'render mode' is derived
  from it rather than independent of it.
• Only the DERIVED half is cached. bundle_id, relpath, ref and size come
  from the request: blobs are deduplicated, so one log hangs off several
  bundles and the cached render has to serve all of them. Pinned by a test.
• Bounded by BYTES, not entries. A 2 KiB diff and a 4 MiB log are both one
  entry, so a count-based bound means nothing. tracker.artifact_cache_bytes
  (default 64 MiB, 0 disables).

A ref with no sha256 -- the fs backend -- is deliberately not cached: the
path's contents can change underneath, so no key stays true. Renders that
errored are not cached either; the cause is usually the file rather than
the bytes, and a transient read failure must not stick to the sha.

DELIVERY SWEEP. Chose the process-wide throttle over the bead's other
option (a separate endpoint the page calls). An endpoint would have meant
reconciliation stops happening until the new UI is written to call it --
a functional regression in the interim, for a view that does not exist
yet. delivery_sync.reconcile_open_deliveries() now does the whole sweep
in one call, throttled by tracker.delivery_sweep_seconds (default 60),
and the worklist calls it once instead of looping. Per-bundle rate
limiting is unchanged, so GitHub is asked no more or less often; what
changed is that the render stops opening one SQLite connection per open
delivery every time anyone loads the page.

Also folded the per-candidate target lookup into the sweep's own query --
the old loop did a SELECT per bundle to find it.

CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING: a merge that lands just after a sweep is
invisible for up to the sweep interval. That is the trade, and it is why
the interval is a setting. reset_sweep_throttle() exists because the
throttle is process-global state that tests asserting reconcile-on-render
have to control -- test_tracker_agentic_views needed it.

description:
The patch loop's turn cap is 30, a hardcoded default on
patch.py:19 (`max_tool_turns: int = 30`). It is not in settings.py, so
it cannot be changed without editing code, and `dportsv3 config show`
does not mention it. steps.py:842 records it as deliberate -- when
_lift_budget_if_free drops the token budget, "max_tool_turns (30, from
patch.py) and tier.max_iterations still bound the loop". So it is a
real backstop, not an oversight. What follows is an argument that 30 is
the wrong number, not that the bound should go.

MEASURED, comms/hamlib 2026-09-04, ASSIST at 600k:

  A  turns  billable  cache%   stop
  1     30    80,797   95.5%   turn cap
  2     30    67,348   97.2%   turn cap
  3     30   215,730   90.9%   turn cap
  4     27    87,863   95.3%   text_only -> rebuild_ok

Four attempts, 451,738 billable of a 600,000 budget. Every attempt that
did not finish stopped on the TURN cap; none stopped on tokens, and
~150k of budget went unspent. The port was fixed, so this is not a hard
port hitting a sensible wall -- it is a solvable port being chopped
mid-step four times.

The closing line of each attempt shows where the cut landed:

  A1 "now deciding between disabling USB support or patching the test
      utility"
  A2 "drops out cleanly when USB is disabled -- but I need to check
      what that costs the core library"
  A3 "a one-line guard suffices -- staging the dragonfly patch"
  A4 "The patch applies cleanly -- prior attempt likely just ran out of
      turns before rebuilding. Time to build."   -> rebuild_ok

One continuous line of work, severed three times at 30 turns. A4 needed
27 turns only because A1-A3 had already done the investigation.

THE SECOND, INDEPENDENT REASON. Each attempt is an unavoidable cold
start: poly-2w6 shipped prompt_cache_key and it hits roughly 1 retry in
3, so an attempt boundary costs ~33k billable two times out of three.
This run paid 98,597 in cold starts plus an 83,111 mid-attempt eviction
-- 40% of its billable -- largely because it needed four attempts. Every
attempt boundary removed is a ~33k dice roll removed.

So the turn cap and the cache interact: a low turn cap forces more
attempts, and more attempts cost more cold starts. Raising the cap
attacks both.

NOT AN ARGUMENT FOR CUTTING max_iterations. That was proposed and
retracted on poly-5e1 -- hamlib needed all four attempts and the fix
landed on the fourth. Fewer attempts is good only if the work finishes
inside them, which is what raising the turn cap is for.

WHAT TO DO
  1. Make it a setting (runner.max_tool_turns or similar) rather than a
     patch.py default, so it can be tuned without a deploy and shows up
     in `config show`. Every other bound in this loop is already a
     setting; this one is invisible.
  2. Raise the default. 30 was not chosen against this evidence.
     Candidate 50-60: A1-A3 each had budget left and were mid-step.
  3. Re-measure hamlib and one other multi-attempt port. The signal to
     watch is attempts-to-fix and total billable, not turns.

CAUTION. The budget gate is checked BETWEEN turns and a single turn can
overshoot it (observed +48% on a 120k tier), so a higher turn cap
raises the worst-case overshoot too. poly-7eh (tool results accumulate
untruncated) is the thing that makes late turns expensive, so these
should be looked at together -- raising the cap without bounding
per-turn growth moves the failure from "chopped early" to "one huge
turn".
design:
DESIGN, settled after reading the code 2026-09-04.

FLAT SETTING, NOT PER-TIER. The obvious-looking home is policy.tiers,
beside max_iterations and max_tokens -- it is the same kind of bound.
Do not. policy.tiers is read as one whole table (_from_tables uses
spec.get(key, 0)), and the live config on the builder overrides it
wholesale:

  [policy.tiers.AUTO]    max_iterations=2  max_tokens=30000
  [policy.tiers.ASSIST]  max_iterations=4  max_tokens=600000
  [policy.tiers.MANUAL]
  [policy.tiers.CONVERT] max_iterations=2  max_tokens=150000

None of those carry a turn field, so a per-tier max_turns would resolve
to 0 on the deployed box the moment it shipped -- an attempt with no
turns at all. That is exactly the trap CLAUDE.md warns about ("read as
one whole table -- a partial override silently discards the rest").
A flat runner.max_tool_turns has no such failure mode. Per-tier is a
later change with a migration, not this one.

THE DEFAULT: 50. Not a round guess -- match it to the budget the tier
already grants. A1 spent 80,797 billable over 30 turns, ~2.7k/turn.
ASSIST's 600k over max_iterations=4 is ~150k per attempt, which at that
rate is ~55 turns. 30 turns can only ever spend ~80k of a 150k
allowance, which is why 150k went unspent on a run that hit the turn
cap three times. 50 lets an attempt actually reach the budget it was
given; the budget then bounds the spend, as it was always meant to.

WHY THIS DOES NOT UNBOUND ANYTHING. The token budget still binds and
still fires first when it is the real constraint -- tool_loop stops on
token_budget independently of max_turns. Raising the turn cap does not
raise the spend ceiling; it stops the loop from ending BELOW that
ceiling. The three bounds remain: max_tokens, max_iterations, and this.

THREADING. patch.py:19 is the only production value; attempt_loop.run
(12) and tool_loop.run (12) are library defaults for direct callers and
should stay. Resolve in patch.py via a None sentinel so an explicit
argument still wins -- the manual harnesses and tests pass their own.

TWO STALE COMMENTS TO FIX with the change, both of which name the
literal 30 and would start lying:
  - settings.py, llm.patch.free_tier: "the patch harness's 30 tool turns"
  - steps.py:842, _lift_budget_if_free: "max_tool_turns (30, from patch.py)"
notes:
SHARPER EVIDENCE THAN THE DESCRIPTION USES.

Turns per attempt, comms/hamlib, the same port run either side of an
unrelated change (poly-5e1's retry handoff) that demonstrably altered
the agent's behaviour:

  OLD:  A1 30   A2 30   A3 30   A4 30    -> patch_gave_up
  NEW:  A1 30   A2 30   A3 30   A4 27    -> agent_fixed

Seven of eight attempts consumed exactly 30. The eighth used 27 because
it FINISHED -- stop reason text_only with rebuild_ok -- not because it
ran out of work.

That is the argument in one table. Change what the agent knows, change
what it spends its turns on, change the outcome from gave-up to fixed,
and the turn count does not move. A model with turns remaining uses
them, so 30 is not a safety margin the agent rarely reaches; it is the
thing that decides when nearly every attempt ends.

CONSEQUENCE: the turn cap is a hard ceiling on progress per attempt,
independent of the token budget (~150k unspent here) and independent of
any improvement to the prompt. No change to what the agent is told can
raise it, because the saved turns are simply reallocated rather than
banked -- measured on poly-5e1, where a handoff that removed a large
amount of re-derivation produced no reduction in turns at all.

This is a cleaner argument than the "chopped mid-step" framing in the
description, which it supersedes. The mid-step evidence is still true
and worth reading -- it shows WHERE the cut lands -- but it invites the
reply "then the attempts should be smarter", and this table forecloses
that: they were smarter, and it changed nothing about when they stopped.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-04, not yet deployed or measured.

  settings.py   runner.max_tool_turns, int, default 50
  patch.py      max_tool_turns: int | None = None, resolved from the
                setting when None so an explicit argument still wins,
                and read per call rather than as a default argument
                (settings are cached per process; a default would
                freeze whatever loaded first)
  steps.py      _lift_budget_if_free's docstring no longer names 30
  settings.py   llm.patch.free_tier's note no longer names 30, and its
                wall-clock arithmetic now scales with the setting
  sample        regenerated

Left alone on purpose: attempt_loop.run (12) and tool_loop.run (12) are
library defaults for direct callers, not production values -- patch.py
is the only production path and always passes.

tests/test_turn_cap_setting.py, 9 tests. tests/test_free_tier_budget.py's
turn test rewrote from `signature(patch.run).default == 30` to the
behaviour it meant: patch.run resolves the setting, passes it down, and
it exceeds attempt_loop's own 12. Pinning the literal is what made it
fail on a value change that was the point of the change.

Mutation-checked: never reading the setting (4 fail), reverting the
default to 30 (1 fail), ignoring an explicit argument (2 fail). Full
suite 3126 passed.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH. The evidence proves 30 was BINDING -- it
ended seven of eight attempts -- not that 50 produces better outcomes.
50 is derived from the budget arithmetic, not measured. Step 3 of WHAT
TO DO still stands and is now the whole remaining task: re-run hamlib
and one other multi-attempt port, and watch attempts-to-fix and total
billable. Two outcomes would argue for reverting rather than tuning:
attempts that now run 50 turns without finishing any sooner, or a
worse budget overshoot per turn (see the CAUTION and poly-7eh).

OPERATIONAL NOTE FOR WHOEVER DEPLOYS. Jobs get longer in wall-clock in
proportion: at the measured 10-30s per turn, an attempt moves from
5-15 minutes to 8-25, and four attempts from ~1h to ~1h40 worst case.
The dsynth gate pauses the runner during builds, so this reduces
throughput per port even where it improves the outcome. Worth watching
alongside the token numbers.
title: the patch turn cap is a hardcoded 30 and it, not the budget, is what ends attempts

description:
Accept makes a decision and performs a side effect in one action, commits
the decision first, and offers no way to re-run the side effect when it
fails. The bundle is left accurate but unactionable.

MEASURED 2026-09-04: 17 bundle_review_requests rows sit at create_failed,
14 of them from the poly-lt1 clone race. Every one names a bundle whose
resolution is already 'accepted' and which has no PR. Recovering each one
means reopening a decision that was never wrong.

ORDER OF OPERATIONS

api_bundle_accept:

  1. UPDATE ... resolution = 'accepted', accepted_at = ?    (committed)
  2. _accept_delivery_step(...)  -> opens the PR

Step 2 failing does not roll back step 1 -- deliberately, since the
create_failed row is the record of what happened. But then
fix_state.py:95 refuses a second attempt:

    "accept": lambda r, v: r not in TERMINAL_RESOLUTIONS and v == VERIFIED

and RESOLUTION_ACCEPTED is in TERMINAL_RESOLUTIONS. The comment above
that set states the consequence plainly: "Terminal decisions -- nothing
acts on these except reopen."

WHY REOPEN IS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT

The operator's decision was correct and is correctly recorded. Only the
side effect failed. Reopen retracts the decision to re-trigger the side
effect, which:

  - loses accepted_at and the bundle_accepted event's meaning
  - re-runs the full accept path, including the same clone acquisition
    that failed, so batching reopens reproduces poly-lt1 immediately
  - reads, in lineage views, as though the fix was un-accepted and
    re-accepted, when nothing about the judgement changed

THE MODEL ALREADY SEPARATES THESE

  - _accept_delivery_step is already a standalone function, not inlined
    in the endpoint.
  - bundle_review_requests carries its own status lifecycle
    (create_failed / merged) independent of bundles.resolution.

So the schema already treats the decision and the delivery as two
things. Only the action layer conflates them.

PROPOSED

A 'deliver' action (endpoint + button) that:

  - is allowed when resolution == 'accepted' AND the newest
    bundle_review_requests row for the bundle is create_failed
  - re-runs _accept_delivery_step and writes a fresh review-request row
  - changes no resolution and emits no bundle_accepted event

It cannot corrupt state the way reopen->accept can, because it never
touches the decision. It also turns the current 14-bundle backlog into
one action each rather than a reopen/accept round trip that re-races the
clone every time.

RELATED, NOT THE SAME

poly-lt1 is why delivery fails (a shared clone with no mutex at the
request layer). This is why an operator cannot recover once it has.
Fixing poly-lt1 lowers the frequency; it does not provide the exit.
Three of the 17 create_failed rows are NOT the race -- GitApplyConflict,
GitCommitError "nothing to commit", GitWrongBranch -- and those need a
regenerated fix rather than a retry, so the action should surface the
error rather than retry blindly.
notes:
REVISITED against the code before implementing. The diagnosis holds; the
shape of the fix is constrained by three things worth recording.

VERIFIED 2026-09-04. All 17 create_failed rows are stranded by the strict
definition — the newest review-request row for the bundle is create_failed
AND bundles.resolution = 'accepted':

    DeliveryError: another delivery is using the clone   14
    GitApplyConflict: git apply --3way produced ...       1
    GitCommitError: nothing to commit ...                 1
    GitWrongBranch: clone is on branch 'agentic/...'      1

1. THE GATE HAS TO SPLIT ACROSS TWO PLACES.

ACTION_ALLOWED entries are `(resolution, verification_status) -> bool`
(fix_state.py:93-104). Delivery status is not in that signature and must
not be forced into it — the module's own contract says the table
"captures ONLY the state gate each endpoint checks today; the endpoint
keeps its metadata/concurrency guards and HTTP shaping."

So: `"deliver": lambda r, v: r == RESOLUTION_ACCEPTED` in the table, and
the newest-row-is-create_failed check in the endpoint, returning 409.

2. THE UI FLAG DOES NOT BELONG IN bundle_actions().

bundle_actions() is documented pure over resolution / verification_status
/ target / origin with no DB access; live reads are merged by the caller
(the verify env-picker precedent, pages.py:325-340). But nothing new is
needed: pages.py:299 already loads `delivery_request` via
latest_review_request_for_bundle for the Delivery card, and
_bundle_delivery.html already branches on `dr.status`. The button is one
more branch in a template that already has the data.

3. THE ERROR IS ALREADY SURFACED.

_bundle_delivery.html renders `dr.error` when present, so "surface rather
than retry blindly" needs no new plumbing — the operator can already see
that a row failed on GitApplyConflict rather than the clone race. Do NOT
string-match the error to block a retry: three of the seventeen are not
the race, but a retry of those is cheap, writes a fresh row with the same
error, and is more honest than a gate guessing which errors are
retryable.

4. THE RETRY MUST NOT PRETEND TO BE AN ACCEPT.

Accept emits `bundle_accepted` + a bundle_accepted activity row and calls
mark_issue_resolving. The retry path must do none of that — the decision
already happened and the issue is already resolving. It should reuse only
_accept_delivery_step, then write the same `delivery_complete` activity
row accept writes (bundle_actions.py:421-434) so the ribbon reads as one
continuous story, plus its own event so the retry is distinguishable from
the original attempt.

5. `skipped` IS A REAL OUTCOME OF THE RETRY.

_accept_delivery_step returns status='skipped' with a skip_reason for
no_config / no_changes_diff / changes_diff_empty / changes_diff_unreadable
/ operator_optout. A retry can legitimately land there (e.g. delivery was
switched off since the accept). Report it as-is rather than treating it
as success or failure.
title: a failed delivery strands an accepted bundle: no PR, and accept refuses to run again

description:
The agent's own build reaches any port in the tree, including every one
excluded from the loop, and nothing bounds how long it takes.

MEASURED, devel/hyprutils, 2026-09-04.

The patch agent investigated the compiler setup -- grep
'USE_GCC|PORT_COMPILER|df.gcc', then get_file on bsd.df.gcc.mk.diff and
bsd.default-versions.mk.diff -- wrote a patch, and called dsynth_build at
06:39:26. Ninety minutes later the job had logged nothing further and the
host was running:

    dsynth -S -y -p 2026Q3 test devel/hyprutils
    dsynth: [00] WORKER package  lang/gcc13

lang/gcc13 is on the feeder's denylist, holds an open origin_skip_flag,
and had already been refused a direct build. It is being built anyway,
as a dependency the agent's own patch introduced.

MECHANISM

worker.py:3252, dsynth_build ->

    dsynth -S -y -p "$DPORTS_DSYNTH_PROFILE" test "$1"

dsynth re-resolves the dependency tree from the Makefile as the agent
just edited it. A patch that adds USE_GCC makes a compiler a build
dependency, and dsynth builds it. The tool takes (env, origin) and
consults nothing else.

WHY THE EXISTING EXCLUSIONS DO NOT COVER IT

  - The feeder previews with `dsynth status <origin>` and refuses a big
    dependency set. That preview reads the port as found on disk, BEFORE
    the agent edits it. The set that actually gets built is the post-edit
    one, which does not exist at preview time. The guard cannot see this
    by construction.
  - origin_skip_flags gate the runner picking up a JOB for an origin
    (confirmed working: devel/llvm19 retired dead, origin_locked). They
    say nothing about dsynth building that origin as somebody else's
    dependency.
  - The denylist regex filters only the feeder's own dtest calls.

NO UPPER BOUND

_exec declares `timeout: int | None = None` (worker.py:1302) and
dsynth_build calls it without one, so subprocess.run gets timeout=None.
There is no ceiling other than how long the largest dependency takes.
llm.patch.timeout (600) bounds the LLM call, not the build.

BLAST RADIUS

The runner pauses while any dsynth is on the host. So one agent's build
stalls every other job on the box -- other patch jobs, and verify jobs an
operator queues meanwhile. The batch feeder blocks behind its drain. A
single agent decision can idle the whole pipeline for hours.

THE FIX IS NOT FLAGS

dsynth -x / -xx ("do not rebuild packages with dependencies which require
rebuilding") would bound it, but poly-8ni established that the loop must
be proved by the gate it is judged by: dsynth test, the same command
verify-fix runs. Weakening the agent's build below the acceptance gate
reintroduces exactly what poly-8ni fixed.

Candidates that keep the gate intact:

  1. Preview before building. Run `dsynth status <origin>` on the EDITED
     port inside dsynth_build, and refuse with a blocked_by reason when
     the plan exceeds a package cap or names an excluded origin. The
     agent already handles blocked_by (stale_compose does this today),
     so a refusal is a turn it can act on rather than a crash.
  2. Give dsynth_build a timeout, so an unbounded build cannot idle the
     host indefinitely. Needs to be generous -- a legitimate large port
     is slow -- but a ceiling is better than none.
  3. Consider whether a patch that introduces a NEW build dependency is
     a fix the loop should accept at all. Every observed case here came
     from the agent reaching for a different compiler rather than fixing
     the code.

Discovered while feeding ports through the loop on hardware.
title: the agent's dsynth_build builds any dependency its own patch introduces, unbounded and unfiltered

description:
Two quantities are both called "tokens" and each display picks whichever
its event happened to carry. Nothing labels which one is on screen.

  billable = uncached prompt + completion   <- what the budget enforces
  total    = prompt + completion, where prompt re-counts the whole
             cached prefix EVERY turn       <- what the provider reports

On one real patch job (audio/cdparanoia, 2026-09-03) they differ by
21x: 86,141 billable against 1,817,637 total. Neither is wrong. They
answer different questions and are presented identically.

THE CLEAREST CASE -- two adjacent lines of the bundle timeline, same
word:

  attempt 1/4 for audio/cdparanoia (tokens used 0/120000)
  attempt 1 for audio/cdparanoia: rebuild_ok=False tokens=1396534
  attempt 2/4 for audio/cdparanoia (tokens used 72041/120000)
  attempt 2 for audio/cdparanoia: rebuild_ok=False tokens=421103

Attempt 1 used 1,396,534 by one line and 72,041 by the next.
attempt_loop.py:243 sends billable as tokens_used_so_far;
attempt_loop.py:386 sends total as tokens; agentic_bundle.html:129,131
renders both as "tokens".

WHERE EACH SITE STANDS

  _job_token_usage.html      billable headline + total marked
                             "incl. re-billed cache"   <- the only
                             one that is right
  agentic_bundle.html:145    port lifetime card: Prompt / Completion /
                             Total only. cdparanoia shows 5,313,167
                             where the port cost 395,837 billable
  render/activity.py:63      activity group total = sum of total_tokens
  agentic_session.html:169   per-turn cumulative_total_tokens, while
                             tool_loop.py:191 emits
                             cumulative_billable_tokens right beside it,
                             unused

So the same job reads as 86k, 1.4M or 5.3M depending on the page.

TWO MORE, found while tracing

1. TRIAGE MEASURES NO CACHING AT ALL. triage.py:132-140 emits an
   llm_turn without cached_tokens; tool_loop.py:186 includes it. The
   Usage object HAS the number, the event drops it. The card then
   computes billable = prompt + completion, so every triage job claims
   a 0% cache hit -- and "no cache" is indistinguishable from "not
   measured".
2. LATENT: token_usage_for_job matches stage LIKE '%llm_turn',
   token_usage_for_port matches stage = 'llm_turn' exactly
   (agentic_queries/jobs.py). Dormant -- no convert:llm_turn rows exist
   today -- but the two cards would disagree silently the moment one
   appears.

The pie is internally consistent (it is a breakdown of total) but
renders as ~95% blue "cached" directly above a Billable row of 86,141,
so the picture is dominated by a number that is not the cost.
design:
ONE UNIT FOR THE HEADLINE, EVERYWHERE: billable. Total stays -- it is
the honest provider number and the ratio between the two is itself the
signal a prefix cache is working -- but it never appears without the
"incl. re-billed cache" qualifier that _job_token_usage.html already
uses. That template is the model; the rest is what it has not reached.

FIX THE TWO WRITERS FIRST. Everything else is a consequence, and
fixing the readers one by one would be chasing symptoms:

  1. runner.py:4087  patch_audit.json's tokens_used gains cached and
                     billable. result.usage already has them. This one
                     change is what lets the PR, the handoff, the
                     proposed fix and the agent's context all report
                     cost instead of re-billed traffic.
  2. attempt_loop.py:386  attempt_end carries billable alongside total,
                     so the bundle timeline can show the same unit as
                     the line above it.
  3. triage.py:132   emit cached_tokens and billable_tokens like
                     tool_loop.py:186 does. Until then triage claims a
                     0% cache hit and _activity_row.html:28 shows a
                     total under a header that says billable.

THEN THE READERS

  4. orchestrator.py:545  the PR says which number it is, or says
                     billable. This one is published upstream, so it
                     matters most and should not wait.
  5. token_usage_for_port returns cached/billable -- it already sums
     the rows it needs -- and the port card leads with billable.
  6. _job_activity.html:108, render/activity.py:63, the session view
     and agentic-bundle.js:427 use the billable figures the events
     already carry.
  7. the two stage matchers agree (LIKE '%llm_turn' vs = 'llm_turn').

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not drop total, and do not "reconcile" the two by
picking whichever is smaller. They measure different things and both
are wanted; the defect is that they are unlabelled and interchanged.

A CARD ONLY SEES llm_turn ROWS. Any spend that is charged to
result.usage without emitting one is invisible to the job card while
still appearing in the audit -- a real 34,682-token divergence was
observed this way. Whatever the fix, keep one source of truth for a
job's cost rather than two sums that can drift.

VERIFY on real jobs, not fixtures: take one patch job and one triage
job and check the card, the activity group header, the audit, the PR
body and the handoff all report the same billable figure.
notes:
RE-REVIEW. This is not a display bug. It starts at two writers and
everything downstream inherits it, including surfaces outside the
tracker.

THE TWO WRITERS

  runner.py:4087-4094  patch_audit.json's tokens_used carries
                       prompt/completion/total and DROPS cached, even
                       though result.usage has it. Every audit consumer
                       is therefore stuck with total.
  attempt_loop.py:386  attempt_end sends attempt_usage.total_tokens as
                       "tokens", while attempt_loop.py:243 sends
                       total_usage.billable_tokens as
                       "tokens_used_so_far". Adjacent events, same word,
                       different units.

description:
Follow-up to poly-2w6, which sent prompt_cache_key and did NOT fix the
retry cold start. This is the piece that does.

WHY THE KEY ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH. The provider matches only the
MOST-RECENTLY-USED prefix for a key. Attempt 1 grows its conversation to
~110k tokens, so that long chain becomes the match target. Attempt 2's
first request shares only the early [system, payload] prefix -- still
cached, an exact repeat of it hits -- but it is not what the lookup
compares against, so attempt 2 pays its whole cold start again.

THE FIX. Before the first request of attempt N>1, send one throwaway
request containing EXACTLY attempt 1's opening messages. Exact matches
hit regardless of recency, so that call is nearly free, and it makes the
early prefix most-recent again. The attempt's real first request is then
a plain extension of it and hits.

MEASURED BY REPLAY of the real cdparanoia transcripts, two arms on
separate keys, chain grown 30 turns so the failure actually reproduces:

  ARM A  attempt2 turn1, no re-prime
         prompt=31269 cached=    0 out=170  BILLABLE=31439
  ARM B  re-prime (max_tokens=1)
         prompt=31172 cached=31153 out=  1  BILLABLE=   20
  ARM B  attempt2 turn1
         prompt=31269 cached=31217 out=271  BILLABLE=  323

  NET SAVING: 31,096 billable tokens per retry, cost 20.

The throwaway completion is NOT a hidden cost: with max_tokens=1 it
emitted one output token: reasoning did not blow through the cap. That
was the open question when the approach was first described.

For scale: cdparanoia's tier budget is 120k and its cold start ~31k, so
attempt 2 currently spends a quarter of the remaining budget re-reading
context it already had. nspr's cold start is 42k, so its saving is
larger. This is the difference between max_iterations: 4 being fiction
and being real.
design:
Send attempt 1's exact opening messages once, before attempt N>1 starts,
with the same prompt_cache_key and max_tokens=1.

Where: attempt_loop, at the top of an attempt when attempt_idx > 1. It
needs the first request's messages from attempt 1, which the loop
already has -- the payload is rebuilt per attempt and the system prompt
is constant, so "attempt 1's opening" is reconstructible without storing
a transcript.

BEST-EFFORT, NON-NEGOTIABLE. Wrap so that any failure -- timeout, 4xx,
5xx, provider change -- is a no-op that does not touch the attempt, does
not consume the budget ladder, and does not log an error louder than
DEBUG. It is an optimisation; nothing may depend on it.

Only for providers whose dialect declares cache controls. Reuse
_CACHE_DIALECTS from poly-2w6: no dialect, no re-prime. DeepSeek has no
key and no most-recent-prefix behaviour to exploit.

MEASURE, do not assume: log the re-prime's own usage and the following
turn's cached_tokens, so the gain is visible per run rather than
inferred from this bead. If a future provider change kills it, that
number goes to zero and says so.

RISKS, both real:

1. UNDOCUMENTED BEHAVIOUR. Most-recently-used matching appears nowhere
   in Meta's docs; it is inferred from measurement. It can change
   silently. The best-effort wrapper is what makes that survivable.

2. THERE IS A REGIME WHERE NONE OF THIS HELPS. The decay probe went cold
   at 30 minutes and never recovered across an hour of continued keyed
   traffic (poly-2w6 notes, behaviour 3, unexplained, n=1). So the tier
   budget must still be sized as though the cache is absent -- this
   reduces cost when it works, it does not make max_iterations safe on
   its own.

NOT WORTH IT WHEN attempts are short: with 20 turns of growth the miss
does not occur and the re-prime is a no-op costing 20 tokens. That is
cheap insurance, not waste, and it is why this should be unconditional
for attempt N>1 rather than gated on a size heuristic nobody can tune.

IMPLEMENTED (uncommitted, NOT yet verified on hardware).

                    key never reaches the endpoint, so a re-prime there
                    would be a full-price request buying nothing.

                    own Usage or None. Never raises: the support check
                    is inside the guard too, because it reads settings.
                    Goes straight to _complete_openai rather than

precisely the leak the budget has to be able to see. Not counting it
would hide a provider change behind a silent overspend.

THE PREMISE IS REFUTED. This bead rests on "an exact repeat hits
regardless of recency". The re-prime was byte-identical to attempt 1

TWO MODELS FIT THE DATA AND I CANNOT SEPARATE THEM AT n=1:

  (b) the cache only serves a request that closely FOLLOWS another on

(b) also fits the decay probe never recovering after 30 minutes, which
(a) never explained. Neither is worth asserting without a designed

WHAT DID NOT REGRESS: the safety design held. The re-prime's true cost
was visible in its own activity row rather than hidden, the budget was
charged 34,682 for it (attempt_start showed 72,041/120,000 going into
attempt 2), and nothing depended on the hit. Charging it is what made
the wash measurable instead of looking like a 34k saving in the turn
rows.

RECOMMENDATION: revert. It buys nothing measurable, costs one extra
request per retry and ~350 tokens, and the assumption underneath it is
now known to be false. Reverting leaves poly-2w6's key in place, which
is still correct and still cheap. The alternative worth more than
another cache trick is the one already noted here: have attempt N
continue attempt N-1's conversation instead of rebuilding it, which
needs no provider assumption at all.
REVERTED in ad6857d. Not a design that needs another pass -- the

  * within-attempt caching works and is worth having (99% hits between

  * the cross-attempt cold start is real and unfixed. cdparanoia pays

    conflicts with the deliberate workspace reset between attempts, so
    it is a real design question, not a trick
  * raising the tier budget remains the blunt instrument that would
    actually move these ports

description:
MEASURED, not inferred. Meta's endpoint caches prefixes, but only routes
you back to the backend holding one if the request carries
prompt_cache_key. We send none, so every request after a divergence is
load-balanced to an arbitrary backend whose auto-cache has never seen
our prefix.

Same ~7.5k-token prefix, five requests, diverging tails:

    1. cold, WITH key                 cached=0
    2. diverging, WITH key            cached=7537   <- hit
    3. diverging, NO key              cached=0      <- key needed to READ
    4. diverging, WITH key again      cached=7537   <- still there
    5. diverging, DIFFERENT key       cached=0

Step 3 is the finding: the prefix demonstrably existed (step 4 hit it
straight after) and a keyless request still could not find it. So
"populate once with a key, then rely on auto-cache" does not work -- the
key must be on EVERY request that wants the cache.

Docs agree with the mechanism: "Requests that share a key route
together, so a request is more likely to land on a backend that already
holds its prefix." Auto-caching is real -- it is why we see 99% hits
between consecutive turns of one attempt -- but across a gap that
affinity is luck, and we measured it losing 6 times out of 6.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE PRICE. Our tier budget counts
billable = raw - cached, so a cached prefix is nearly free against the
BUDGET, not just the bill. Cold-start size predicts budget exhaustion
almost perfectly across 11 ports run 2026-09-03:

    34702  net-snmp         budget_exhausted
    33823  cdparanoia       budget_exhausted
    31904  timidity         fixed
    25770  libfyaml         fixed

    24172  google-perftools fixed

    17806  cdb              fixed

fixed. At 120k, a 33k cold start leaves ~87k and a second attempt costs

on four separate runs under two different models.

A working cross-attempt cache turns attempt 2's cold start from
24k-42k billable into a few hundred, which is the difference between
1.4 attempts and the 4 that max_iterations already promises. No prompt
changes, no budget increase.
design:
Send a stable prompt_cache_key on every request, per provider that has
the concept.

SCOPE: Meta only. DeepSeek's caching is automatic with no equivalent
knob (prefix-only from token 0, 64-token chunks, reported as
prompt_cache_hit_tokens/prompt_cache_miss_tokens). So this belongs
beside _REASONING_DIALECTS as a second per-provider capability, not as a
blanket parameter -- sending an unknown field to deepseek is exactly the
400 that _reasoning_meta exists to avoid.

WHAT THE KEY SHOULD BE. One stable key per group of requests that share
a prefix. A per-bundle key fixes the retry case; a key per (role,
playbook selection) would also let different ports share the static
prefix. Since a bundle's attempts share their playbook selection too,
the coarser key subsumes the finer one -- and at one-job-at-a-time
volume, pinning all traffic to one backend is what we want, not a
scaling risk. Simplest workable version: one key per role,
e.g. "polytropos-patch". Nothing is stored or expires; the key is
derived, never persisted, because it is a routing hint and not a handle.

Also set prompt_cache_retention: "24h". It is documented as a hint, not
a guarantee ("the server may evict entries early under load"), so treat
it as opportunistic. A decay probe measuring real survival time is
running; if the prefix does not survive the gap between attempts, this
bead only helps within an attempt and the tier budget stays the real
constraint.

TWO IMPLEMENTATION TRAPS, both verified against the current code:

1. extra_body COLLISION. _complete_openai does
       kwargs.update(_reasoning_kwargs(reasoning, provider))
   and _reasoning_kwargs returns {"extra_body": {...}} for deepseek-off
   and for nvidia. A cache-key addition that also sets extra_body will
   clobber the reasoning payload via .update(). The two must MERGE into
   one extra_body dict, and a test should pin that -- silently losing
   `thinking: disabled` would restore the ~50% reasoning spend poly-r1g
   exists to cut.

2. THE SDK IS TOO OLD FOR THE NAMED KWARG. openai 1.70.0 on the box
   raises "Completions.create() got an unexpected keyword argument
   'prompt_cache_key'". Both parameters have to go through extra_body,
   which is also why trap 1 is unavoidable rather than incidental.

PLUMBING. llm.complete() takes no context identifier today, and neither
does tool_loop.run() (messages, model, env, api_base, api_key,
custom_llm_provider, timeout, max_turns, max_tokens, on_event,
attempt_idx, tool_whitelist, reasoning). A role-level constant needs no
plumbing at all, which is a further argument for the coarse key over a
per-bundle one.

attempt 2 turn 1 reports a large cached_tokens instead of 0. That single
number is the whole bead.

kwargs.update(_reasoning_kwargs(...)), and both tables return an
extra_body: deepseek-off sends `thinking`, nvidia sends
`chat_template_kwargs`, Meta's cache controls go there too. A plain
update() drops whichever ran first -- and losing `thinking: disabled`
silently restores the ~50% of billable spend poly-r1g exists to cut.

model routes together, which is what we want at one-job-at-a-time
volume: a bundle's attempts share a prefix and so do different ports up
to their first divergence. It needs no plumbing at all -- llm.complete()
and tool_loop.run() carry no context id, so a per-bundle key would have
meant threading an argument through both for no measured gain.
