Re-ran the four budget-exhausted ports with the key deployed:

  devel/nspr         budget_exhausted  30 turns  1 attempt
  net-mgmt/net-snmp  budget_exhausted  30 turns  1 attempt
  audio/cdparanoia   budget_exhausted  36 turns  2 attempts  A2T1 cached=0/34372
  databases/redis    budget_exhausted  30 turns  1 attempt

Identical to the run before the change. nspr hit exactly 30 turns for
the fifth time.

WHAT DOES WORK, so this is not a regression:
  - the key IS on the wire (verified against the deployed build:
    extra_body carries prompt_cache_key + retention, merged correctly
    alongside reasoning_effort)
  - within-attempt caching is unchanged: cdparanoia attempt 1 turn 2
    cached 34225/34521, turn 30 cached 57329/57684

WHAT FAILS: attempt 2 turn 1, cached=0, on a request that is
BYTE-IDENTICAL to attempt 1 turn 1 (system 19,076 chars identical, user
89,540 chars identical), sent 9 seconds after attempt 1's last turn and
4.9 minutes after attempt 1's first.

FOUR HYPOTHESES TESTED AND DISPROVEN, each with a measurement:
  1. Time-based eviction -- no: 4.9 minutes, well inside the 20 the
     decay probe held.
  2. Extension supersedes the short form -- no: primed a short prefix,
     extended it 8 times, re-sent the short form, still hit 4977/5021.
  3. Prompt size -- no: an 85k-token prompt repeated hit 85169/85211.
  4. Tools, or cross-port contention on the shared key -- no: tools do
     not change prompt_tokens or break the hit, and the activity log
     shows cdparanoia ran alone from 11:04 to 11:09 with no interleaving.

UNEXPLAINED: attempt 2 turn 1 reports 34,372 prompt tokens where
attempt 1 turn 1 reported 34,275 -- a 97-token difference on messages
that are byte-identical. Tools are not in the session transcript, and
they do not affect prompt_tokens in a direct test, so the delta's source
is not yet identified. It is the most promising thread: something
outside the recorded messages differs between attempts, and whatever it
is sits early enough to end the prefix match.

THE COMMIT MESSAGE OVERCLAIMED. It says "This is budget, not just
price". On this evidence the budget claim is unsupported: the mechanism
is real and measurable in isolation, and does not reach the case it was
built for. The change is harmless and correct in itself -- keep or
revert on taste -- but the tier budget remains the actual constraint on
these four ports, and raising max_tokens is back on the table as the
thing that would actually move them.
ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is deterministic -- the earlier "probabilistic,
n=1" reading was wrong.

THE PROVIDER MATCHES ONLY THE MOST-RECENTLY-USED PREFIX FOR A KEY, not
every cached prefix.

Reproduced end to end with the real transcripts:

    state: large chain (30 grown turns)   prompt= 84175  cached=81521
    branch WITHOUT re-prime               prompt= 31269  cached=0
    re-prime: exact [sys,user]            prompt= 31172  cached=31153
    branch AFTER re-prime                 prompt= 31269  cached=31217

During attempt 1 the conversation grows to ~110k tokens, so the
most-recent entry for the key is that long chain. Attempt 2's first
request shares only the early [system,user] prefix. That prefix is still
cached -- an exact repeat of it hits 31,153 -- but it is not what the
lookup compares against, so the attempt-2 branch gets nothing. Touch it
first and it becomes most-recent again, and the branch then hits 99.8%.

This explains every observation at once:
  - within-attempt hits: each turn extends the most-recent chain
  - attempt-2 miss: shares only the early prefix
  - synthetic 30-turn test hit: growth was ~1k, so the early prefix was
    still effectively the most recent
  - exact-repeat probes hit: exact match works regardless of recency

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX IT: before the first request of attempt N>1,
issue a throwaway "cache touch" with the exact prefix attempt 1 opened
with. That call is itself ~99.9% cached -- 31,172 prompt, 31,153 cached,
so ~19 billable tokens plus a minimal completion -- and it converts the
attempt's 24k-42k cold start into near zero.

CAVEAT worth weighing before building it: most-recent-prefix matching is
NOT documented anywhere. It is inferred from measurement and could
change without notice. A re-prime call is cheap and harmless if the
behaviour changes (it just stops helping), but it is one extra request
per attempt and it encodes an assumption about provider internals. The
alternative -- having attempt N continue attempt N-1's conversation
rather than rebuilding it -- needs no provider assumption at all, but
attempts deliberately reset the workspace, so that is a bigger change.
DECAY PROBE COMPLETED, and its tail is unexplained.

    [1m..20m]  keyed 5169/5226   unkeyed 0
    [30m]      keyed    0/5226   unkeyed 0
    [45m]      keyed    0/5226   unkeyed 0
    [60m]      keyed    0/5226   unkeyed 0
    [90m]      keyed    0/5226   unkeyed 0

It never recovered. Every probe re-sends the same prefix WITH the key,
so each should re-prime and the next should hit -- which is exactly what
the re-prime experiment showed happening within seconds. Instead the key
went cold at 30 minutes and stayed cold for an hour of continued keyed
traffic.

So there are now three measured behaviours:
  1. keyed prefixes hit reliably at short range        (reproduced many times)
  2. only the MOST-RECENTLY-USED prefix is matched     (reproduced deterministically)
  3. a key can stop hitting entirely and not recover   (observed once, unexplained)

(1) and (2) are solid. (3) contradicts a simple model of (1) and (2) and
has n=1. It may be backend rotation, a per-key lifetime, or the unkeyed
control call in the probe interfering.

BEARING ON THE RE-PRIME FIX: the fix targets a gap of seconds between
attempts, which sits well inside where behaviour (1) holds, and the
reproduction was unambiguous. But (3) means none of this should be
depended on -- a re-prime must be best-effort, cost nothing when it
misses, and the tier budget must still be sized as though the cache is
absent. Anything that only works when the cache hits will fail in
whatever regime (3) represents.
WHOLE-RUN COST BREAKDOWN, comms/hamlib 2026-09-04, 600K tier.
Four attempts, agent_fixed, 451,738 billable total:

   A  turns   prompt_in     out   billable  cache%   worst turn
   1     30   1,540,378  12,112     80,797   95.5%   32,146 (T1)
   2     30   1,563,631  23,907     67,348   97.2%    6,348 (T8)
   3     30   1,750,607  55,743    215,730   90.9%   83,111 (T25)
   4     27   1,337,447  25,546     87,863   95.3%   33,432 (T1)

Every cache miss in the run:

   triage T1  in=16296 (cached=0)  billable=18817
   A1.T1      in=32058 (cached=0)  billable=32146   cold start
   A3.T1      in=32928 (cached=0)  billable=33019   cold start
   A3.T25     in=78758 (cached=0)  billable=83111   <- mid-attempt
   A4.T1      in=33264 (cached=0)  billable=33432   cold start

Three cold starts at ~32-33k = ~99k, 22% of the run, spent purely
re-establishing a prefix. Add the T25 eviction and roughly 40% of the
run's billable went to cache behaviour.

NEW, AND IT EXTENDS THIS BEAD: A3.T25 is a MID-ATTEMPT eviction. This
bead says auto-caching within an attempt is real -- "it is why we see
99% hits between consecutive turns of one attempt". That holds on
average (90.9-97.2% here) but it is not guaranteed: turn 25 of 30, on
an unbroken conversation, came back cached=0 and re-billed the whole
78,758-token prefix. One turn, 83,111 billable, 39% of that attempt.

So the exposure is not only "each attempt pays a cold start". Any turn
can drop, and the later it drops the more it costs, because the prefix
it re-bills has grown. A 30-turn attempt is 30 chances to lose the
affinity coin-flip, and prompt_cache_key is what would stop it.

Note also A2, the only attempt with NO cold-start miss -- it inherited
A1's warm cache and cost 67,348 against A1's 80,797. Net of cold
starts A2 is actually the more expensive of the two (67,348 vs
48,651), so the apparent saving was cache luck, not attempt economics.
Worth remembering when reading any per-attempt cost comparison: with a
32k cold start on a 600k budget, cache noise is larger than most
effects being measured.
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-09-04, comms/hamlib. Closing.

This bead named its own test: "check that attempt 2 turn 1 reports a
large cached_tokens instead of 0. That single number is the whole
bead." It passed:

  A1.T1  in=32058  (cached=0)      billable=32146   expected, first request
  A2.T1  in=32867  (cached=31985)  billable=989     <- the test, passed
  A3.T1  in=32928  (cached=0)      billable=33019
  A4.T1  in=33264  (cached=0)      billable=33432

Implementation is complete: 5d4be30 on master, deployed, 13 tests in
tests/test_llm_prompt_cache.py. Both traps handled -- _merge_call_kwargs
merges extra_body rather than clobbering the reasoning payload, and both
parameters go through extra_body because SDK 1.70.0 rejects them as
kwargs. provider=meta, llm.backend=auto, so the SDK path is taken and
the key is on the wire.

BUT THE BENEFIT IS PARTIAL, ~1 HIT IN 3 RETRIES. When it lands it is
emphatic (33,019 -> 989 billable, 97%). Two of three retries still paid
a full cold start, seconds after the previous attempt ended. Three
things narrow it: the misses are TOTAL, not partial, so it is routing
rather than prefix divergence -- a divergence would still hit the shared
~32k of system+payload; timing is not it, the gaps were seconds against
a decay probe that held 98.9% through 20 minutes; and nothing of ours
was competing, no other LLM traffic between 17:51 and 18:21.

This is consistent with poly-b05, which is already closed: its revert
found a BYTE-IDENTICAL repeat missing too. Whatever causes the miss is
provider-side routing the key does not reliably control. There is no
further code fix available on our side, which is why this closes rather
than staying open.

KNOWN DEVIATION, recorded not actioned: the DESIGN above says "one key
per role, e.g. polytropos-patch". The code ships polytropos-{model}, and
all three roles (triage, patch, chat) are configured to the same model,
so they share one key and can evict each other under an interleaved
feeder. Not fixed because poly-b05's byte-identical-repeat result says
prefix contention is not the mechanism, so separating the keys would not
buy what this bead is about. Revisit only if a measurement implicates
role contention specifically.

NEW FAILURE MODE, see the note above: the cache can drop MID-attempt.
A3.T25, turn 25 of 30 on an unbroken conversation, came back cached=0
and re-billed 78,758 tokens for 83,111 billable. This bead assumed
within-attempt caching was reliable ("99% hits between consecutive turns
of one attempt"). It is not.

CONSEQUENCE, and where the remaining value is: if each attempt is an
unavoidable ~33k dice roll, the lever is FEWER ATTEMPTS. This run paid
98,597 in cold starts plus the 83,111 eviction -- 40% of its 451,738
billable -- because it needed four attempts, all four of which died on
the TURN cap with ~150k of budget unspent. Raising max_turns is the
actionable follow-on.
title: the prompt cache is unreachable across requests: no prompt_cache_key is sent, so every attempt re-pays its cold context

description:
`github.deliver` drives a single shared `delivery.clone_dir` through
checkout -> apply -> commit -> push -> restore. The Accept endpoint is a
sync FastAPI route, so uvicorn runs each request in its own threadpool
thread. Nothing serialises them. Two Accepts a few seconds apart overlap
in the clone.

Observed 2026-09-02. Clone reflog:

    18:45:47  checkout: master -> agentic/irc-ircd-ratbox-2026Q3-...
    18:45:48  commit: irc/ircd-ratbox: fix build failure on DragonFly
              <- 18:45:50.93 math_arpack-ng@openmpi Accept refuses here
    18:45:53  reset: moving to HEAD          } restore_to_base
    18:45:54  checkout: ...ratbox -> master  }

bundle_review_requests rows bracket it: id=19 arpack-ng create_failed at
18:45:50.937 with

    GitWrongBranch: clone is on branch 'agentic/irc-ircd-ratbox-2026Q3-...',
    expected base_branch 'master'

and id=20 ircd-ratbox created at 18:45:54.294. The push is the slow leg
(~5s) and is the window.

The refusal is the guard working, not the bug. `prepare_clean_branch`
asserting clean+on-base is the only thing that stopped arpack-ng's diff
being committed onto ircd-ratbox's branch and force-with-lease pushed
there, silently corrupting an already-accepted PR. The bug is that a
shared mutable resource has no mutex.

Recovery today is a plain retry once the clone is idle: the finally-block
restore does run, so the clone returns to base on its own.
design:
Serialise deliveries on the clone. Candidate shapes, simplest first:

(a) module-level threading.Lock keyed by clone_dir in the git driver.
    Correct for today's deployment: one uvicorn process, no --workers.
    Smallest diff. Does not cover a second process (a CLI-driven
    delivery, or a future worker count > 1).

(b) fcntl.flock on a lockfile inside the clone, wrapping github.py's
    whole prepare -> push -> restore span, bounded wait so a hung
    delivery reports "another delivery holds the clone, retry" rather
    than blocking the request thread. Covers any process. clone_dir is
    already documented as dedicated to delivery, so it is the natural
    mutex key.

(c) queue accepts and deliver from one worker. Largest change; only
    worth it if delivery grows other shared state.

Not yet chosen -- pick the simplest that actually holds. Whichever wins,
the lock must span the restore, not just the prepare: the window that
bit us was between commit and restore.
notes:
Implemented: one module-level threading.Lock in orchestrator, held
across the whole provider.create_review_request call.

Chosen over the file lock originally sketched, on facts: deliver() has
exactly one caller (the Accept route) and uvicorn.run() is invoked
without `workers`, so every delivery is a thread in one process. A
cross-process lock would defend against a process that cannot exist
today.

Bounded wait, not blocking: anyio's default thread limiter is 40
(verified in the installed anyio), so an unbounded wait behind one hung
delivery would park request threads until the tracker stops answering.
Waits delivery.git_timeout -- an existing setting, no new knob and no
env var -- which is 60s against a measured 7s healthy delivery.

The timeout raises DeliveryError from inside deliver()'s existing try,
so a busy clone records the same create_failed row as any other
provider failure, with a message saying to retry.

Lock spans the HTTP calls too, necessarily: restore_to_base runs in
create_review_request's finally, i.e. after the PR is created, so the
clone is still on the feature branch during those calls.

Tests: tests/test_delivery_clone_lock.py (6). The last one reproduces
the incident against real git -- two deliveries started on a barrier
against one real clone -- and fails 5/5 runs with the lock removed.

Residuals, deliberately not coded for:
- If the tracker process dies mid-delivery the lock dies with it and
  the clone can be left on the feature branch. That is a crash, not a
  race; the next Accept refuses, which is the safe direction.
- If anyone adds uvicorn `workers` or a second delivering process, the
  in-process lock stops being sufficient. The assumption is stated in
  the comment above the lock.
REVISITED 2026-09-04. The mutex described in NOTES is present, correct,
and working. What is still hurting is a different problem underneath it,
and the bead title no longer describes it.

MEASURED, the 2026-09-04 11:14-11:16 accept burst:

  delivered ok      12
  clone-timeout     14

Gaps between consecutive SUCCESSFUL deliveries, in seconds:

  6.7  7.7  6.6  7.1  6.8  7.0  7.0  8.2  7.5  7.5  7.1

That is the lock doing exactly its job: one delivery at a time, ~7s
each, no interleaving, no GitWrongBranch. The original race is fixed.

WHAT ACTUALLY FAILED

Not a race. Queueing past a deadline. _clone_locked waits
delivery.git_timeout (60s) and then raises. At ~7s per delivery the
clone serves roughly eight in that window; an operator accepting ~26 in
one sitting pushes the rest past 60s and every one of those is recorded
as create_failed. The first failure lands at 11:15:12.699, ~60s after
the burst began, and the 14 failures interleave with ongoing successes
at 11:15:15 / 11:15:22 / 11:15:30 -- the signature of a queue draining
while latecomers time out, not of contention.

SO THE RECORD IS WRONG

`create_failed` means the provider was asked and refused. Here the
provider was never asked: the delivery did not fail, it was never
attempted. That mislabelling is what stranded 14 accepted bundles with
no PR (poly-86t) and made an operator think 14 fixes had been rejected
upstream.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT

Delivery is synchronous inside the Accept request and serialised, so
accept latency is O(queue depth x 7s) with a 60s cliff. Two consequences
beyond the failures:

  - Each waiting accept parks a Starlette threadpool thread. anyio's
    default limiter is 40 (the figure this bead's own NOTES cite as the
    reason the wait is bounded). A 26-accept burst holds ~26 of them.
  - Raising delivery.git_timeout is not the fix: it is shared with the
    git subprocess timeouts one layer down, so loosening the lock wait
    also loosens those.

CANDIDATE FIXES, given the mutex is already in place

  (a) A separate, larger bound for the lock wait only. Smallest change,
      does not conflate with git_timeout. Still parks request threads
      and still has a cliff, just a further-away one.
  (b) Stop recording a busy clone as create_failed. It is a distinct
      outcome -- not attempted -- and with poly-86t's retry now shipped
      the operator has an exit. Honest record, no throughput gain.
  (c) Make delivery asynchronous: Accept records the intent, a poller
      delivers. This is exactly the verify_requests shape already in
      the codebase (tracker INSERTs a row, runner polls and acts), and
      poly-fij notes that shape also lets a remote runner serve it.
      Removes the cliff and the parked threads entirely. Costs Accept's
      inline delivery outcome, which the UI currently surfaces.

(c) is the one that actually removes the failure mode; (a)+(b) together
are the cheap version that stops the mislabelling and moves the wall.
Not choosing here -- the decision changes Accept's contract.
CLOSING. The race is fixed and now verified on production data.

The threading.Lock recorded in the earlier note is present
(orchestrator.py:63) and demonstrably working: across the 2026-09-04
accept burst, successful deliveries are spaced 6.7 7.7 6.6 7.1 6.8 7.0
7.0 8.2 7.5 7.5 7.1 seconds apart -- strictly one at a time, no
interleaving, and no GitWrongBranch since 2026-09-02.

One change landed here today, because it belonged to this bead's
mechanism: the wait had been borrowing delivery.git_timeout, which
bounds a single git subprocess. They are different quantities that
happened to share the number 60. Split out as
delivery.clone_wait_timeout (300s), so the queue an operator can build
by accepting in bulk went from about eight deep to about forty, without
loosening every git call to get there.

What this bead is NOT about, and is now poly-vxx: a clone that is busy
past that bound is still recorded as create_failed -- a provider failure
the provider never saw -- and delivery is still synchronous inside the
Accept request, so the wall moved rather than went away.
title: Two concurrent Accepts race on the one delivery clone; the loser fails with GitWrongBranch

description:
Two worklist ports have failed identically in every run: the patch job
refuses before the agent is invoked, so the port cannot be fixed by the loop at
all.

  patch refused: could not compose <origin> before starting. The compose tree
  is shared across jobs, so proceeding would work against whatever the previous
  job left there. Underlying error:
  extra: {"rc": 2}

REPRODUCTIONS

Four, across two runs about eight hours apart, on exactly the two worklist
ports that have no overlay.dops in DeltaPorts:

  databases/libvalkey   run 1 and run 2
  sysutils/ucored       run 1 and run 2

Every other worklist port with an existing overlay passed this preflight. The
correlation is with "no overlay", not with load: run 2 happened with the queue
otherwise idle, after concurrent build activity had been stopped.

SEQUENCE

  1. triage runs normally and classifies the failure
  2. triage bootstraps a `type=port` header overlay (new_port) because none
     exists -- "proceeding to patch"
  3. the patch job's preflight calls materialize_dports (steps.py, "Compose
     this one origin BEFORE the agent touches anything")
  4. that returns rc=2 and the job refuses by design: "a compose that did not
     work means we do not know what is on disk"

The refusal is correct behaviour given a failed compose. The bug is that the
compose fails at all, deterministically, for a port whose overlay the harness
itself just created.

WHAT THE COMPOSE ACTUALLY SAYS

Reproduced by hand, and the two ports do not fail the same way:

  sysutils/ucored      rc=2   [fail] preflight_validate: changed=0 skipped=0
                              warnings=0 errors=1
  databases/libvalkey  rc=1   Traceback ... io.open(self, mode, buffering,
                              encoding, errors, newline)

So there is at least a validation failure and an unhandled exception behind the
same refusal, and neither reaches the operator: the message interpolates
`stderr_tail or error`, both empty, so "Underlying error:" prints nothing and
only rc survives into extra.

The bootstrapped overlay is a bare header with no ops:

  port databases/libvalkey
  type port
  reason "Step 48 bootstrap: deterministic header; patch authors the body"
  target @any

NOT THE MISLABELLING BEAD

poly-e75 / poly-jg9 cover the verdict: any harness refusal is recorded as
agent_gave_up, with no patch.md and no patch_audit.json, which reads as "the
agent tried and could not fix it". That is a separate defect from this one and
they are independently fixable:

  fix only the label  -> these ports stay permanently unfixable, honestly named
  fix only this       -> they get a real patch attempt, while provider outages
                         keep being blamed on the agent

RELATED

poly-3sq -- bootstrap overlay stubs left behind in the shared DeltaPorts
checkout when a job does not land. Same bootstrap path; these refusals are one
way a job fails to land. 38 such untracked stubs were counted in the checkout
today, and they block `dev-env update` from fast-forwarding it.
notes:
DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED 2026-09-03 by validating the description against the
code. The description's central claim -- "the compose fails at all,
deterministically, for a port whose overlay the harness itself just
created" -- is WRONG, and the two different rc values it reports were a
red herring.

Compose does not fail on these ports. Run right now, through the exact
code path the preflight uses (worker.materialize_dports, which is just
`reapply <origin>`):

    sysutils/ucored      ok=True rc=0
    databases/libvalkey  ok=True rc=0

Both succeed. Nothing about the bootstrapped header is unacceptable to
compose.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM: the overlay is not there when the patch job looks.

  PORTS_DIR      = /work/DeltaPorts   (a SYMLINK)
  PORTS_MAIN_DIR = /work/ports-main   (the shared checkout)

  1. Triage has NO worktree. _checkout_bundle_branch_for_job has exactly
     one call site, runner.py, and it passes job_type="patch". So triage
     runs with /work/DeltaPorts -> ports-main.
  2. _ensure_overlay_or_abort writes the header with
     worker.put_file(env, "/work/DeltaPorts/ports/<origin>/overlay.dops")
     -- landing in ports-main, UNTRACKED and uncommitted.
  3. The patch job calls create_job_worktree, which does
     `git worktree add` a fresh tree from the base branch and then
     _point_ports_link repoints /work/DeltaPorts at that worktree.
  4. `git worktree add` does not carry untracked files. The overlay the
     harness just wrote is not in the new tree.
  5. materialize_dports composes a port with no overlay -> fails ->
     preflight refuses.

Verified, not inferred:
  - the ports link currently resolves to ports-main (which is exactly
    why a manual reapply succeeds and the real job does not)
  - git status in ports-main shows the bootstrapped overlays untracked:
        ?? ports/databases/libvalkey/
        ?? ports/misc/libuuid/
        ?? ports/sysutils/ucored/
  - 42 untracked stubs in that checkout now

SO poly-3sq IS THE SAME BUG, seen from the other end. The stubs are not
"left behind when a job does not land"; they are orphaned by design at
step 3 of every single bootstrap, because the writer and the consumer
look at different trees. Fixing this fixes the accumulation too.

Also corrected: the description says this reproduces on "exactly the two
worklist ports that have no overlay.dops". The population is wider --
misc/libuuid hit it tonight as a third. It is every port with no
overlay, i.e. every port the bootstrap path exists to serve.

WHY THE ORIGINAL HAND-REPRODUCTION SHOWED rc=2 AND rc=1: not
reinvestigated, and no longer load-bearing. Those runs were made before
the poly-cpd compose fix landed. The rc values in the description should
not be treated as evidence of anything.
IMPLEMENTED. The patch job now establishes its own overlay state, which
is the same principle the compose preflight already states: "each
attempt responsible for its own starting state instead of trusting an
ordering that spans two modules".

  worker.ensure_bootstrap_overlay(env, origin) -- writes the
  deterministic header if the tree PORTS_DIR points at right now has no
  overlay. Idempotent, so a no-op for every port that never needed a
  bootstrap. Called from the patch preflight between assert_port_clean
  and materialize_dports.

  worker.BOOTSTRAP_REASON / worker.read_status_type -- moved out of
  runner so triage and the preflight emit a byte-identical header from
  one source. Read through runner's existing function-level `worker`
  import; a module-level one would have been the only such import in
  that file.

DELIBERATELY BEST-EFFORT. The first cut refused the job when the
bootstrap failed, and four runner-parity tests caught it: that adds a
SECOND refusal path for a condition the compose already gates, so an
unreachable env would start failing with a different message than the
one operators know. It now records what happened
(patch_overlay_bootstrapped / patch_overlay_bootstrap_failed) and lets
the compose arbitrate. Those four tests then passed unmodified, which is
the signal the design was wrong rather than the tests.

Tests: tests/test_patch_bootstrap_overlay.py (6) plus 4 ordering tests
in test_patch_preflight_compose.py. Mutation-verified both ways --
removing the preflight call fails 3, and removing the overlay_dops guard
(so it clobbers real overlays) fails 1. Suite 2972 passed.

STILL OPEN, and unchanged by this: triage keeps writing its bootstrap
into the shared checkout, where it stays untracked and orphaned. That is
poly-3sq's accumulation (42 stubs counted now, up from 38). This fix
makes the orphan harmless rather than fatal; whether triage should stop
writing entirely is the poly-3sq decision, not this one.

NOT YET VERIFIED ON HARDWARE. The three ports that hit this tonight
(databases/libvalkey, sysutils/ucored, misc/libuuid) are the real test
and need a deploy first.
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-09-03, after deploying a41d8bb and re-raising
the three ports that hit this.

All three success criteria met:

  patch_preflight_compose_failed   0   (was 3 of 3)
  patch_overlay_bootstrapped       3   ("re-established type=port
                                        bootstrap overlay in this job's
                                        worktree")
  llm_turns on the patch job       21 / 30 / 49   (was 0 / 0 / 0)

The model had never once been invoked for any of these ports across
three prior runs. It now is.

  databases/libvalkey   agent_gave_up (never invoked) -> agent_fixed, 21 turns

close_reason: A failed verification now leaves three durable records: analysis/verification.log uploaded by the orchestrator, and verification_exit_code + verification_reason persisted on the bundle so the page can say what happened without fetching an artifact. The reason is composed from apply-and-build's own stage exits and stderr tail. The summary is gated on verification_status instead of verification_at, so a failed bundle stops claiming it was verified.
description: Verification is the only failure path in the pipeline that keeps no evidence. An operator can see THAT verify failed and never why. WHAT IS STORED POST /api/bundles//verification writes three columns: verification_status, verification_at, verification_applied_diff_sha256. There is no column for a reason, an exit code, or a log reference. `dsynth_exit` IS accepted in the request body -- documented as "optional, kept for audit" -- and is then forwarded only into the bundle_verified SSE event payload. It is never persisted, so nothing can query or render it. The endpoint docstring names the missing piece itself: "The dsynth log itself is not stored here -- Slice 3 may upload it as a bundle artifact (e.g. analysis/verification.log) via the artifact-store endpoint independently." That slice never landed. WHY THE EVIDENCE IS GONE BY THE TIME ANYONE LOOKS Two perishable copies, no durable one: - dev-env apply-and-build writes work/artifacts/apply-and-build-.log and verify-fix deletes it on success. Sampling every env after two failed verifies found none present. - dsynth's per-port log under work/dsynth/logs/ is overwritten by the next build of that origin. Establishing why devel/libunwind failed verification took an ssh session and a read of a log the next build would have destroyed. It had to be done twice. The answer -- check-sanity rejecting the port over ineffective options helpers, nothing to do with the fix under test -- was worth having: it was poly-cpd, and the loop had been patching the wrong file for five bundles because of it. A CONTRADICTION IN THE SUMMARY _bundle_summary.html renders {% if bundle.verification_at %} verified {{ bundle.verification_at }} {% endif %} verification_at is set on BOTH outcomes -- the endpoint writes it whether ok is true or false. So a failed bundle shows the red "verify failed" pill from fix_status() and, two lines away, "verified 2026-09-02T13:38:13". The wrong one looks authoritative because it carries a timestamp. SHAPE OF THE FIX - Upload the apply-and-build log as analysis/verification.log on failure. The endpoint already names the path; the artifact store already takes uploads. - Persist the exit code and a short reason next to verification_status so the bundle page can say what happened without fetching an artifact. - Gate the summary line on verification_status, not verification_at, so a failed verification stops claiming it was verified. Verification is the gate an operator accepts a fix on. It is the one place where "it failed, work out why yourself" is most expensive.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-05. All three parts of the bead's fix shape.

1. DURABLE LOG. verify_fix uploads the apply-and-build log as
analysis/verification.log on failure only, before POSTing the verdict.
Best-effort: a failed upload must not lose the verdict, so it warns and
carries on. The endpoint's docstring had named this exact path as
something 'Slice 3 may upload'; it never landed, which is why a failed
verify kept no evidence at all.

2. EXIT CODE AND REASON PERSISTED. Two new bundles columns
(verification_exit_code, verification_reason) plus MIGRATIONS entries,
verified against a database created before them. dsynth_exit was already
accepted and documented as 'kept for audit', then forwarded only into the
SSE payload -- accepted and dropped. The reason is READ OFF the
apply-and-build result rather than guessed: it reports which stage
refused (git apply / reapply / dsynth) and a stderr tail, so
_failure_reason composes 'dsynth exited 1: check-sanity: ineffective
options helper' -- which is exactly the answer that cost an ssh session
to find. Bounded at 2000 chars server-side; the column holds a reason,
not a log.

3. THE SUMMARY NO LONGER CONTRADICTS ITSELF. _bundle_summary.html gated
on verification_at, which the endpoint writes on BOTH outcomes, so a
failed bundle showed the red 'verify failed' pill and 'verified
<timestamp>' two lines apart. Now gated on verification_status, and the
failed branch shows the exit code inline.

ALSO: made _put_artifact an injectable hook on run_verify_fix, matching
_get_json/_get_bytes/_post_json. Without it the existing failure-path
tests would have attempted real HTTP to the fake tracker URL.

Nine tests: four on the orchestrator (uploads on failure, uploads nothing
on success, a failed upload keeps the verdict, the reason names the
stage), three on the endpoint (exit code and reason persisted, reason
bounded, no false 'verified' in the summary), plus the two updated.
title: a verify failure records no reason anywhere, and the bundle summary still says 'verified' when it failed

description:
poly-8ni gave the agent dsynth_test so it could reach the acceptance
gate. It does. The refusal is then discarded, because reporting it depends on
the model emitting a Patch Log it may never reach.

OBSERVED

devel_libunwind-20260902-124214Z, first run after poly-8ni deployed:

  turn 19  dsynth_build  rebuild_ok=true
  turn 22  dsynth_test   rebuild_ok=false   <- gate refused
  turn 23  dsynth_log
  turns 24-30  get_file / grep / list_dir   <- diagnosing the refusal
  turn 30 = max_tool_turns (patch.py)

The attempt hit the turn cap mid-investigation and never emitted a final
response. analysis/patch.md is 205 characters of mid-reasoning. The
proof-block orphan rescue in attempt_loop then lifted rebuild_ok=true from
the turn-19 dsynth_build result and synthesized

  {"rebuild_ok": true, "source": "tool_result"}

so the bundle resolved agent_fixed with no record anywhere that the gate had
refused it. Verify will refuse it again, for the same defect, with the loop's
own evidence already discarded.

WHY THE PROMPT IS NOT ENOUGH

The patch prompt asks the agent to name a gate refusal in Patch Log and stop.
That instruction can only run if the model gets a turn to write the report.
Here the gate landed at turn 22 of 30 and the refusal was ambiguous enough to
investigate -- reasonable behaviour, since the agent cannot tell immediately
whether the failure is its own. Any instruction whose execution competes with
the turn budget will be dropped exactly when the news is most interesting.

The harness does not have this problem. The dsynth_test result is in the tool
trace; nothing needs to be remembered or re-derived.

FIX DIRECTION

Record the gate outcome harness-side, next to rebuild_ok:

- track dsynth_test results in the tool loop the way rebuild_ok_seen already
  tracks dsynth_build
- carry it into the proof dict on both paths -- the model-authored proof block
  and the synthesized orphan-rescue one -- so analysis/rebuild_proof.json
  gains a gate field that is present regardless of what the model wrote
- surface it in the tool-trace summary so the next attempt's payload shows the
  gate refused, not just that a build passed

Then the prompt instruction becomes a nicety rather than the mechanism.

A prompt guard capping post-gate investigation is worth adding too, but on its
own it only narrows the window; it does not close it.

NOTE ON SCOPE

This does not change what agent_fixed means -- see poly-8ni for why requiring
a green gate is not yet safe. It makes a refusal visible to the operator and
to the next attempt.
title: a dsynth_test refusal is lost when the attempt hits the turn cap, so an observed gate failure still reports agent_fixed

description:
The agent's success oracle and the acceptance gate run different
builds, so a bundle can be resolved agent_fixed and then fail verification for
a defect the loop had no way to observe.

MECHANISM

Patch loop: worker.dsynth_build runs `dsynth build` directly with -S -y (its
docstring says dbuild is intentionally not used). rebuild_ok comes from that
exit status, and rebuild_ok is what marks a bundle agent_fixed.

Verify gate: dev-env cli.py apply_and_build step 3 runs `dtest`, i.e.
`dsynth test`. Per helpers.py that "exercises the extra Q/A phases (stage-qa,
check-plist, the test target) AND force-rebuilds by removing any existing
package first". It also runs with DEVELOPER=1.

DragonFly's Mk/bsd.sanity.mk gates its whole DEV_ERROR block on
`.if defined(DEVELOPER)`. So a class of Makefile defects is fatal under the
gate and invisible to the loop.

FIRST CONFIRMED INSTANCE

devel/libunwind-20260902-103058Z. Patch agent: rebuild_ok=true, one attempt,
resolution agent_fixed. Verify: two runs, both `dsynth stage exit=1`, both
dying at check-sanity:

  The following options helpers are incorrectly set after bsd.port.options.mk
  and are ineffective: TESTS_CONFIGURE_OFF TESTS_CONFIGURE_ON

The underlying Makefile defect is poly-cpd (mk eval appended after the options
include) and is pre-existing -- the agent's diff only adds a static patch file
and one `file materialize` line. The build dies before the patched file is ever
compiled, so the fix was neither proved nor disproved.

WHY THE AGENT CANNOT SEE IT

No agent tool runs `dsynth test`. The 18-tool surface has dsynth_build and
dsynth_log only. The loop cannot reach the gate it is judged by, and the
verify failure is not fed back into the bundle, so a re-attempt starts from the
same blind spot and would produce the same green result.

FIX DIRECTIONS

- Set DEVELOPER=1 in the agent's dsynth_build. Cheapest; surfaces DEV_ERRORs
  during the loop. Does not cover the QA phases or the force-rebuild.
- Add a dsynth_test tool and require it as the final proof for a fix the agent
  wants to call done. Closes the gap properly; every attempt gets more
  expensive, and stage-qa/check-plist failures become the agent's problem.
- At minimum, write the verify failure back onto the bundle so a re-attempt
  sees why acceptance was refused instead of re-deriving a green build.

Worth deciding deliberately: making the loop's build identical to the gate is
not obviously right -- the cheap build is what makes iteration affordable.
Surfacing the delta may be better than closing it.

ALSO

dev-env cli.py apply_and_build's docstring says it runs `dbuild ORIGIN`; the
code runs `dtest`. Stale doc, same function.
title: patch loop proves fixes with dsynth build but acceptance gates on dsynth test, so DEVELOPER/QA defects pass the loop and fail verify

description:
`agent_gave_up` is recorded whether the agent gave up or the harness never
reached the model. The two are indistinguishable afterwards, and the second
case is the common one.

MEASURED 2026-09-02 across the full tracker history (136 bundles):

  resolution            with analysis/patch.md   without
  agent_fixed                    18                 0
  agent_gave_up                   3                32
  agent_budget_exhausted          1                 8

Artifact retention is NOT the explanation. agent_fixed bundles have their
patch.md on every day in the window, including the oldest (20260829). The
absence is specific to the give-up verdicts, and spans every day:
20260830 0/14, 20260831 1/9, 20260901 0/8.

A genuine give-up is a real agent output: the patch prompt asks for
`## Rebuild Status: gave-up` plus a next-step recommendation in Patch Log, and
that lands in analysis/patch.md. A bundle marked agent_gave_up with no patch.md
never got that far.

OBSERVED DIRECTLY tonight. archivers_lz4json-20260902-002241Z was marked
agent_gave_up at 03:49. Its entire history is provider rate limiting - four
patch attempts, each ending `Harness patch failed ... Error code: 429`. The
agent did real work (make_patch, get_file, dupe, edit_file, genpatch) and never
once concluded anything. Its patch.md and patch_audit.json return
`{"error": "artifact not found"}`.

WHY IT MATTERS

The resolution is the only durable record of what happened. Anything reasoning
about agent quality reads it:

- An operator triaging the queue sees "the agent gave up on lz4json" and
  concludes the port is hard. It is not; the provider was down.
- Any claim of the form "the agent fails on N% of ports" is unfounded, because
  the denominator mixes model failure with infrastructure failure.
- poly-3aa sampled the agent_fixed side and is unaffected, but the same style of
  analysis applied to the give-up side would be measuring the provider.

This is adjacent to poly-4av (a transient provider error kills the job) but it
is a different defect. poly-4av is about the job dying; this is about the
death being misattributed to the agent in the permanent record.

PROPOSED

Separate "the agent concluded it could not fix this" from "we could not run the
agent". A distinct terminal resolution for infrastructure failure - provider
error, env broken, harness crash - would do it. The evidence to decide is
already present at the point the resolution is written: a give-up that produced
no patch.md is not a give-up.

Do not backfill silently. The 32 existing rows should be treated as unknown
rather than relabelled, since the underlying cause is no longer recoverable for
most of them.
notes:
SECOND LIVE CONFIRMATION 2026-09-02 06:21.

math_xspread-20260902-043007Z resolved agent_gave_up. Its analysis/patch.md and
analysis/patch_audit.json both return {"error": "artifact not found"}. Its
history is the same as lz4json's: triage completed, then patch attempts cut off
by HTTP 429, never reaching a rebuild.

Two different ports, same night, same false verdict. Running count is 33 of 36
agent_gave_up bundles with no patch.md, against 18 of 18 agent_fixed that have
one.
SCOPE REFINEMENT 2026-09-02 06:30. Distinguishing misnamed from merely
evidence-free, so the fix targets the right rows.

  resolution               with report   without   name honest?
  agent_fixed                  18           0      yes
  agent_gave_up                 3          33      NO - asserts the agent decided
  agent_budget_exhausted        1           8      partly - budget is a harness
                                                   condition, and running out
                                                   mid-attempt explains a missing
                                                   report
  triage_failed                 0           4      yes - says triage failed, does
                                                   not claim the agent concluded
                                                   anything

The defect is specifically agent_gave_up. It is the only verdict that attributes
a decision to the model while carrying no evidence the model ever spoke. 33 of 36.

triage_failed and agent_budget_exhausted are evidence-free too, but they name a
harness condition rather than an agent judgement, so they mislead far less. They
do not need renaming; agent_gave_up does.

New data point: net-mgmt_ipv6mon-20260902-043028Z resolved triage_failed at 06:29
straight after `Harness triage failed ... Error code: 429`. Its analysis/triage.md
returns {"error": "artifact not found"}. Correctly named, and the honest contrast
with lz4json and xspread on the same night is what makes the agent_gave_up naming
indefensible.
THIRD CONFIRMATION 2026-09-02 08:27. security_libfido2-20260902-043053Z
resolved agent_gave_up after `Harness patch failed ... Error code: 429`.
analysis/patch.md returns {"error": "artifact not found"}.

Three ports in one night - archivers/lz4json, math/xspread, security/libfido2 -
all marked as the agent giving up, none of which reached the model's conclusion.
Running count 34 of 37, against 18 of 18 agent_fixed with a report.
